tech-quantum-practice.title: Quantum computing III · hardware, security & careers
tech-quantum-practice.description: Real quantum hardware in general terms, noise and error correction, reading Qiskit-style code, QKD and NIST post-quantum cryptography with a simulated TLS inventory, careers, and a programme final with mock interviews. Part 3 of the Quantum programme.

courses.title: Quantum hardware in general terms
courses.summary: How real qubits are built: superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photons and spins, with honest trade-offs and the key numbers engineers compare.
outcomes: Learners can describe the main qubit modalities
Learners can compare coherence, gate speed and connectivity
Learners can explain why superconducting chips need dilution refrigerators

lessons.title: Lab: Explore a superconducting qubit system

scenes.text: Visiting a lab, Neha sees a golden 'chandelier' hanging from the ceiling.
It is a dilution refrigerator; the chip at the bottom sits around 10–20 millikelvin.

steps.title: Superconducting qubits
steps.body: Circuits of aluminium/niobium with Josephson junctions behave like artificial atoms (e.g. the transmon). Controlled by microwave pulses; gates take tens of nanoseconds.

steps.title: Why so cold
steps.body: The qubit energy gap is a few GHz, tiny compared with room-temperature heat. Millikelvin temperatures keep thermal noise from flipping qubits.

steps.title: Trade-offs
steps.body:
- Fast gates, fabricated like chips
- Limited nearest-neighbour connectivity
- Coherence typically tens to hundreds of microseconds

steps.title: Not a magic box
steps.body: Most of the hardware is control electronics, wiring and cooling, not the chip.

activity.prompt: Explore a simplified dilution-refrigerator stack. Tap each stage from room temperature down to the chip.

objects.label: Room-temperature plate
objects.info: Vacuum can top; control cables enter here from racks of microwave electronics.

objects.label: ~4 K stage
objects.info: Cooled by a pulse-tube cryocooler. Amplifiers for readout often sit near here.

objects.label: Still (~1 K)
objects.info: Part of the helium-3/helium-4 dilution cycle.

objects.label: Mixing chamber (~10 mK)
objects.info: Coldest stage, where the mixture of helium isotopes removes heat.

objects.label: Qubit chip
objects.info: Superconducting qubits with Josephson junctions, shielded from magnetic fields and stray light.

objects.label: Attenuated coax lines
objects.info: Microwave control lines are filtered and attenuated at each stage to block heat and noise.

story.title: Five ways to build a qubit

scenes.text: Each lab in the conference uses a different qubit.
None wins on every metric yet.

steps.title: Trapped ions
steps.body: Charged atoms held by electromagnetic fields in vacuum; lasers or microwaves drive gates. Very high fidelities, long coherence, all-to-all connectivity in a chain, but slower gates and scaling challenges.

steps.title: Neutral atoms
steps.body: Atoms held in optical tweezers; entangled via Rydberg states. Large, reconfigurable arrays.

steps.title: Photonics
steps.body: Qubits in light; many components work at room temperature, natural for networking. Challenges: photon loss and probabilistic two-photon interactions; detectors are often cryogenic.

steps.title: Spin qubits
steps.body: Electron spins in silicon quantum dots; potentially compatible with chip fabrication; still early in scale.

courses.title: Noise and quantum error correction basics
courses.summary: Where errors come from, how repetition and surface codes detect them without measuring the data, the threshold idea, and what 'logical qubit' really means.
outcomes: Learners can name bit-flip, phase-flip and readout errors
Learners can compute logical error rates for a repetition code
Learners can decode a 3-qubit syndrome
Learners can explain thresholds and surface-code overhead

scenes.text: Ideal Bell counts are 50/50 on 00/11; hardware shows 01 and 10 too.
Noise comes from the environment, control errors and readout.

steps.title: Error types
steps.body:
- Bit flip (X error)
- Phase flip (Z error), from dephasing (T2)
- Amplitude damping (T1 decay)
- Readout error (0 read as 1)
- Leakage and crosstalk

steps.title: Mitigation vs correction
steps.body: Error **mitigation** post-processes noisy results (e.g. readout calibration, zero-noise extrapolation). Error **correction** encodes logical qubits in many physical ones and fixes errors during the computation.

steps.title: Myth
steps.body: Mitigation does not make arbitrarily long computations possible; correction is needed for that.

activity.prompt: Sort each technique

items.text: Running extra calibration circuits and rescaling results

options: The measurement reports the wrong bit

scenes.text: If each bit flips with p, the code fails only if 2 or 3 flip.

steps.title: Logical error
steps.body: P_L = 3p²(1−p) + p³ = 3p² − 2p³. For p = 0.01: 0.000298, about 34× better than one bit.

steps.title: Break-even
steps.body: Encoding helps only when P_L < p, i.e. p < 0.5 for this code. Real codes have lower thresholds because gates and measurements also fail.

steps.title: Phase flips
steps.body: The bit-flip code does nothing against Z errors. Shor's 9-qubit code and the surface code handle both.

activity.prompt: Decode a classical 3-bit repetition-code readout by majority vote.
activity.starter:
bits = input().strip()   # three physical bits read from a repetition code, e.g. 010
# TODO: majority vote -> print the logical bit 0 or 1
print(0)
activity.solution:
bits = input().strip()
ones = bits.count("1")
print(1 if ones >= 2 else 0)

quiz.q: The bit-flip code fails when… bits flip.
Which errors does the 3-qubit bit-flip code NOT correct?
options: Any X error on one qubit

scenes.text: You can't read the data qubits: that would destroy superposition.
Instead measure parities Z₀Z₁ and Z₁Z₂ with ancilla qubits.

steps.title: Syndrome table
steps.body: (Z₀Z₁, Z₁Z₂) parity: (0,0) no error · (1,0) flip q0 · (1,1) flip q1 · (0,1) flip q2.

steps.title: Surface code
steps.body: Data and measure qubits on a 2D grid; distance-d code uses about 2d² − 1 physical qubits per logical qubit (d² data + d² − 1 measure). Below a threshold of roughly 1% physical error, increasing d suppresses logical errors exponentially.

steps.title: Milestone
steps.body: In 2024 Google reported a surface-code memory on its Willow chip whose logical error fell as code distance grew, an important below-threshold demonstration.

activity.prompt: Given 3 bits (a bit-flip pattern on 000), compute both parities and print the syndrome and which qubit to flip.
activity.starter:

s2 = 0  # TODO: parity of qubits 1 and 2

activity.solution:

s1 = b[0] ^ b[1]
s2 = b[1] ^ b[2]

courses.title: Reading Qiskit-style code
courses.summary: Read, predict and debug the kind of Python quantum code you'll meet in tutorials and jobs: circuits, measurement, bit ordering, transpilation and results.
outcomes: Learners can read QuantumCircuit code and draw the circuit
Learners can predict counts including bit ordering
Learners can spot common bugs
Learners can explain transpilation and shots

scenes.text: qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2); qc.h(0); qc.cx(0, 1); qc.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])
With 1,000 shots, what will the counts look like?

steps.title: Read line by line
steps.body:
- QuantumCircuit(2, 2): 2 qubits, 2 classical bits
- h(0): Hadamard on qubit 0
- cx(0, 1): CNOT control 0, target 1
- measure([0,1],[0,1]): qubit i → bit i

steps.title: Prediction
steps.body: A Bell state: about 500 '00' and 500 '11' (ideal). On hardware, a few '01'/'10'.

steps.title: Bit order
steps.body: Qiskit bitstrings are little-endian: qubit 0 is the RIGHTMOST character. qc.x(0) then measure prints '01'.

activity.prompt: A circuit is QuantumCircuit(1,1); h(0); measure(0,0) run with 4,000 shots on an ideal simulator. About how many '1' counts do you expect?

steps.title: Common bugs
steps.body:
- Forgetting measurement (no counts)
- Measuring before the last gates
- Wrong qubit indices or reversed bit order
- Angles in degrees instead of radians
- Reusing a classical bit for two qubits

steps.title: Debug by simulation
steps.body: Use an exact statevector simulator first, then shots, then noisy simulation, then hardware.

courses.title: Quantum cryptography: BB84 and QKD
courses.summary: How quantum key distribution uses measurement disturbance to detect eavesdroppers, with a BB84 sifting lab, the 25% error signature and the real-world limits.
outcomes: Learners can run BB84 sifting
Learners can compute the error rate an intercept-resend attacker causes
Learners can list QKD's practical limits
Learners can distinguish QKD from post-quantum cryptography

scenes.text: Alice sends random bits in random bases (Z: |0⟩/|1⟩, X: |+⟩/|−⟩).
Bob measures in random bases; they publicly compare bases, not bits, and keep matches.

steps.title: Protocol (Bennett & Brassard, 1984)
steps.body: 1. Alice picks random bits and bases. 2. Bob picks random bases. 3. Compare bases over an authenticated public channel. 4. Keep bits where bases match (~50%). 5. Sacrifice some to estimate errors. 6. Error correction and privacy amplification.

steps.title: Sifting
steps.body: Bits 1 0 1 1, Alice Z X X Z, Bob Z Z X X → keep positions 1 and 3 → key '11'.

steps.title: Authentication
steps.body: The classical channel must be authenticated, or a man-in-the-middle wins.

activity.prompt: Implement sifting: three input lines give Alice's bits, Alice's bases and Bob's bases. Print the sifted key.
activity.starter:
alice_bits  = input().split()
alice_bases = input().split()
bob_bases   = input().split()
# TODO: keep Alice's bit only where the bases match (sifting)
key = []
print("".join(key))

tests.stdin:
1 0 1 1
Z X X Z
Z Z X X

0 1 1 0 1
X X Z Z X
X Z Z Z Z

activity.solution:
alice_bits  = input().split()
alice_bases = input().split()
bob_bases   = input().split()
key = [b for b, a, c in zip(alice_bits, alice_bases, bob_bases) if a == c]
print("".join(key))
activity.hint: key = [b for b, a, c in zip(alice_bits, alice_bases, bob_bases) if a == c]

quiz.q: Fraction of bits kept after sifting is about…

scenes.text: Eve measures each photon in a random basis and resends it.
In the sifted key she causes about 25% errors.

steps.title: Why 25%
steps.body: Eve picks the wrong basis half the time; then Bob gets a random result, wrong half the time: ½ × ½ = ¼.

steps.title: Detect
steps.body: If Alice and Bob compare 200 sifted bits and see ~50 errors, abort. Typical honest QBER on real links is a few percent.

steps.title: Privacy amplification
steps.body: Below a security threshold (around 11% for BB84 in standard proofs), they can still distil a shorter secret key.

lessons.title: Lab: QKD in the real world

scenes.text: Satellite experiments (e.g. China's Micius, launched 2016) distributed entangled photons over 1,000+ km.
Fibre links lose photons; long networks often use trusted relay nodes.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body:
- Photon loss limits fibre distance to roughly hundreds of km without trusted nodes
- Needs dedicated hardware and an authenticated channel
- Implementation attacks on detectors have been demonstrated
- Gives key exchange only, not signatures

steps.title: QKD vs PQC
steps.body: QKD uses physics and special hardware. Post-quantum cryptography is new maths running on ordinary computers. Several national security agencies currently prefer PQC for most uses.

steps.title: Not unbreakable in practice
steps.body: 'Provably secure' applies to the ideal protocol; real devices have side channels.

courses.title: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
courses.summary: The NIST post-quantum standards (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA), why lattices, hybrid TLS, key sizes, and a practical migration lab with a simulated TLS inventory.
outcomes: Learners can name the 2024 NIST PQC standards and their roles
Learners can explain why RSA/ECC must be replaced
Learners can compare key sizes
Learners can run a crypto inventory and plan a migration

scenes.text: NIST published FIPS 203, 204 and 205 in August 2024.
They replace public-key schemes that Shor would break.

steps.title: The three standards
steps.body:
- **FIPS 203 ML-KEM** (from CRYSTALS-Kyber): key encapsulation, lattice-based (Module-LWE)
- **FIPS 204 ML-DSA** (from CRYSTALS-Dilithium): digital signatures, lattice-based
- **FIPS 205 SLH-DSA** (from SPHINCS+): stateless hash-based signatures, conservative backup

steps.title: What stays
steps.body: Symmetric crypto (AES) and hashes (SHA-2/SHA-3) stay; use larger parameters (AES-256) for long-term security against Grover.

steps.title: Not quantum
steps.body: PQC algorithms run on classical computers; no quantum hardware is needed.

activity.prompt: Match the standard to its role

scenes.text: X25519 public key: 32 bytes. ML-KEM-768 public key: 1,184 bytes; ciphertext 1,088 bytes.
Browsers already deploy hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM key exchange.

steps.title: Hybrid
steps.body: Combine a classical and a post-quantum KEM so the session stays secure if either holds. Common today in TLS 1.3 as X25519MLKEM768.

steps.title: Size ratio
steps.body: 1,184 ÷ 32 = 37: the PQ public key is 37× larger, but still small enough for a TLS handshake.

steps.title: Gotchas
steps.body: Larger ClientHello messages have broken some old middleboxes; test your network path.

steps.title: Inventory
steps.body: List every protocol, library, certificate and stored key: TLS, VPN, SSH, code signing, databases, HSMs, vendors.

steps.title: Prioritise
steps.body: Long-lived secrets and long-lived systems first (Mosca's rule: if secrecy time + migration time > time to a large quantum computer, act now).

steps.title: Roles
steps.body:

- Quantum error-correction researcher: coding theory, PhD often

- Photonics engineer
- PQC / security engineer: classical crypto + migration

lessons.title: Lab: Mock interview · Quantum software engineer (fresher)

scenes.text: A startup interviews Ravi for a junior quantum software role.
Five rounds: concepts, simulator design, Grover, Shor/PQC and a behavioural question.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Define → explain → example → limits. Draw a circuit if you can.

steps.title: What they assess
steps.body: Correct fundamentals, clear communication, testing habits and honesty about hype.

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body: Saying 'a qubit is 0 and 1 at the same time' with no maths behind it.

rounds.q: Explain what a qubit is to a software engineer who knows only classical bits.
rounds.model: A qubit is a two-level quantum system described by a unit vector α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ with complex amplitudes. Measuring it gives 0 with probability |α|² and 1 with |β|², and afterwards the state is the observed basis state. Gates are unitary matrices that rotate the state, which I picture on the Bloch sphere. The power comes from interference between amplitudes, not from storing many answers at once.
followups: What is the difference between global and relative phase?

rounds.q: Write out how you would implement a single-qubit gate on qubit t in an n-qubit state-vector simulator.
rounds.model: I store 2ⁿ complex amplitudes. For every index i whose bit t is 0, I pair it with j = i | (1 << t), read both old amplitudes, and write U applied to that pair back. That is O(2ⁿ) per gate. I test it with known circuits like H·H = I and the Bell state.
followups: How would you implement CNOT?
How does memory scale at 30 qubits?

rounds.q: How does Grover's algorithm work and how many iterations would you use for N = 1,024 and one solution?
rounds.model: Start in a uniform superposition. The oracle flips the sign of the marked state and the diffusion operator reflects all amplitudes about their mean; together they rotate the state by 2θ toward the solution, where sin θ = 1/√N. The optimal count is about (π/4)√N, so for N = 1,024 about 25 iterations. More than that overshoots and the success probability falls.
followups: What changes with multiple solutions?

rounds.q: What does Shor's algorithm threaten, and how would you advise a company today?
rounds.model: Shor's algorithm factors and computes discrete logarithms efficiently, which breaks RSA, Diffie–Hellman and elliptic-curve cryptography, but only on large fault-tolerant machines that don't exist yet. Because recorded traffic can be decrypted later, I'd advise a cryptographic inventory, prioritising long-lived data, piloting hybrid key exchange with ML-KEM and planning signature migration to ML-DSA, with crypto-agility throughout.
followups: What about AES?

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you found a bug in your own analysis. How did you catch it?
rounds.model: In my simulator project, my Bell circuit gave the right probabilities but my QFT output had wrong phases. I wrote a test comparing against a direct DFT formula and found I had the qubit ordering reversed. I fixed it, documented the convention, and added the test to CI so it couldn't regress.
followups: What would you do differently?

tips: Be honest about hype and limits

quiz.q: Best structure for a technical answer:
When unsure in an interview you should…
options: Say what you know and how you'd find out

lessons.title: Lab: Mock interview · Quantum / PQC engineer (mid)

scenes.text: A security team interviews Meera for a PQC migration role with quantum background.
Scenario-heavy rounds.

steps.title: Scenario answers
steps.body: Diagnose → contain → fix → verify → prevent.

steps.title: Signals
steps.body: Numbers, verification steps and stakeholder communication.

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body: Overclaiming timelines for quantum threats.

rounds.q: A Bell-state experiment on hardware shows 8% of counts in 01 and 10. Walk me through your diagnosis.
rounds.model: First I'd separate readout from gate errors by running calibration circuits for |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩ and building a readout matrix. Then I'd check the transpiled circuit for extra SWAPs and the device's current CNOT error on those qubits. Running a noisy simulation with the backend's noise model tells me whether 8% is expected. If not, I'd move to better qubits or report a calibration issue.
followups: How would you verify entanglement, not just correlation?

rounds.q: Explain the surface code's threshold and why logical qubits need so many physical qubits.
rounds.model: The surface code places data and measure qubits on a grid and repeatedly measures parity checks; the syndromes reveal errors without measuring the logical information. A distance-d patch uses about 2d² − 1 physical qubits and corrects up to ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ errors. If physical error rates are below a threshold of roughly 1%, increasing d suppresses the logical error rate exponentially, so we trade many physical qubits for one reliable logical qubit.
followups: What is a decoder?

rounds.q: Our TLS handshakes fail for some branch offices after enabling hybrid ML-KEM. What do you do?
rounds.model: Hybrid ML-KEM makes the ClientHello larger, and some older middleboxes mishandle it. I'd capture traffic at an affected branch, confirm where the handshake breaks, and identify the device. Short term, allow a controlled fallback for that path; long term, update or replace the device with the vendor. I'd continue a staged rollout with monitoring.
followups: How do you avoid weakening security with fallback?

rounds.q: Why are you interested in quantum technology, and how do you keep up with it honestly?
rounds.model: I'm drawn to quantum because it combines linear algebra, physics and engineering, and the security side has real urgency today. I follow peer-reviewed papers and preprints, official standards like NIST's, and I try to reproduce results in simulation. I'm sceptical of press releases and always ask what the classical baseline is.

rounds.q: Design a 2-week benchmark comparing QAOA with classical MaxCut heuristics.
rounds.model: I'd generate graph families of increasing size, compute exact optima for small ones by brute force, and run strong classical heuristics like simulated annealing or Goemans–Williamson. Then QAOA at p = 1–3 in simulation and on hardware, measuring approximation ratio, wall-clock time and total shots. I'd report all results including where QAOA loses.
followups: How do you pick γ and β?

tech-scenes-showcase.title: 3D Tech Scenes — showcase
tech-scenes-showcase.description: Interactive 3D labs: take apart a phone and a PC, follow a chip from wafer to package, see honest shadows of 4D–8D shapes and move a qubit on the Bloch sphere — plus a hardware mock interview.

courses.title: How a smartphone is built
courses.summary: Take a modern phone apart in 3D — layer by layer — and learn what every part does, why it is placed where it is, and how repair technicians open one safely.
outcomes: Learners can name the main layers of a smartphone from back cover to cover glass
Learners can explain what the SoC, RAM, storage and power-management chips each do
Learners can describe why lithium-ion batteries need careful handling
Learners can put the steps of a safe battery replacement in order

lessons.title: Lab: Take a phone apart (exploded view)

scenes.text: Riya dropped her phone. The screen still works but the back glass is cracked, and she wonders what is actually inside.
At the repair shop, the technician says: "A phone is a sandwich of about ten layers. Let me show you."

steps.title: A stack of layers
steps.body:
From the back to the front a phone is roughly: **back cover → charging coil → cameras, battery and main board → metal mid-frame → display → cover glass**.

Each layer is glued or screwed to the next, which is why phones are thin but hard to open.

steps.title: Why the battery is so big
steps.body: The battery is the largest single part — often more than a third of the inside. Everything else is squeezed around it, because battery life matters most to users.

steps.title: How to use the 3D model
steps.body: Press **💥 Explode** to pull the layers apart, drag to turn the phone, and tap any part to read about it. The parts list on the side does the same with a keyboard or screen reader.

activity.prompt: Explode the phone and find the four parts below. Tap a part to read what it does.

tasks.goal: Find the chip with the CPU, GPU and AI engine (the SoC)
Find the memory stacked on top of the SoC
Find the layer that actually makes the light you see

quiz.q: Which part is usually the largest inside a phone?
quiz.why: The battery takes the most space; the other parts are arranged around it.

quiz.q: Why is the back of many phones made of glass rather than metal?
options: Metal would block the wireless-charging magnetic field
Glass is cheaper than every metal
Metal makes phones heavier than glass in all cases
quiz.why: Wireless (Qi) charging works by magnetic induction, which a solid metal back would block.

quiz.q: In an OLED display, what makes the light?
options: Each pixel makes its own light
quiz.why: OLED pixels are self-emissive, so a black pixel is simply switched off.

quiz.q: What sits between the internals and the display?
quiz.why: The aluminium (or steel/titanium) mid-frame is the structural skeleton; the display is glued to its front.

lessons.title: Lab: The chips on the main board

scenes.text: Arjun's phone has 4 GB of RAM and struggles with many apps open. His friend's phone with the same storage feels faster.
The difference is not storage space — it is the SoC and the RAM working together.

steps.title: The main board is a small city
steps.body: The main board carries the **SoC** (CPU cores, GPU, NPU, image processor, often the modem), **RAM** stacked on top of it, **UFS flash storage**, a **power-management IC** and the **RF front-end** for 4G/5G, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.

steps.title: RAM vs storage
steps.body: RAM is the fast desk you work on; it forgets everything when power goes. Storage (UFS flash) is the cupboard: slower, but it keeps your photos and apps with the power off. More storage does not make a phone faster; more and faster RAM and a better SoC do.

steps.title: Do not judge by one number
steps.body: Marketing loves single numbers ("8 cores!", "108 MP!"). Real speed depends on the whole design — chip process, cooling, software and memory.

activity.prompt: Explode the phone and find each chip on the main board. Read its info card before moving on.

tasks.goal: Find the chip that controls charging and power rails
Find the port used for charging and data

tour.text: The main board carries almost every chip.
The SoC is the brain.
RAM sits right on top of it (package-on-package).
Storage keeps data with the power off.
The power-management IC feeds every chip the voltage it needs.

quiz.q: Which memory keeps your photos when the phone is switched off?
quiz.why: Flash storage is non-volatile; RAM is volatile.

quiz.q: Why is phone RAM often stacked directly on the SoC?
options: To keep the wires short and fast
quiz.why: Package-on-package stacking shortens the connections, which saves power and allows higher speed.

quiz.q: What does the power-management IC do?
options: Converts battery voltage into the supply rails chips need and controls charging
quiz.why: It regulates power for every chip and manages charging.

options: The SoC usually contains the CPU, GPU and image processor
More storage always makes a phone faster
RAM keeps data after power is off
The SIM tray contains the CPU
quiz.why: A system-on-chip integrates many processors on one die.

lessons.title: Capstone lab: Replace a phone battery safely

scenes.text: A customer brings a phone whose back cover is bulging. The battery inside has swollen.
The senior technician stops the trainee from prying it open with a metal screwdriver: "Puncture a lithium cell and it can catch fire."

steps.title: Lithium-ion safety first
steps.body: A damaged, punctured or swollen lithium-ion cell can go into **thermal runaway** — it heats itself and can burn violently. Never puncture or bend it; use plastic tools; work on a non-flammable surface; keep a fire-safe container nearby. A swollen battery should be handled by a professional repair shop.

steps.title: Disconnect first, always
steps.body: Inside, the very first electrical step is to **disconnect the battery connector** from the board, so nothing is powered while you work.

steps.title: Disposal
steps.body: Old lithium batteries must go to an e-waste or battery collection point — never in household rubbish, where they can start fires in trucks and dumps.

activity.prompt: Put the steps of a safe battery replacement in the right order.
items: Back up the phone and switch it off
Remove the SIM tray
Gently warm the back-cover edge to soften the adhesive
Lift the back cover with a suction cup and plastic picks
Disconnect the battery connector from the main board
Release the battery adhesive (pull tabs) without bending the cell
Fit the new battery and reconnect it
Power on and test charging before sealing
Apply new adhesive and close the phone
Take the old battery to an e-waste collection point

quiz.q: What is the first electrical step after opening the phone?
quiz.why: Disconnecting the battery makes the rest of the work safe.

quiz.q: Why use plastic tools near the battery?
options: Metal tools can puncture or short the cell
quiz.why: Punctures and short circuits can trigger thermal runaway.

quiz.q: Where should an old lithium battery go?
options: An e-waste or battery collection point
quiz.why: Proper recycling prevents fires and recovers materials.

quiz.q: Why test the phone before sealing it?
options: So a fault can be fixed without opening it again
quiz.why: Re-opening a sealed phone risks more damage.

questions.q: Which part of a phone makes it possible to charge without a cable?
questions.why: The coil receives energy by magnetic induction.
One chip holding CPU, GPU, NPU and more.

questions.q: Which memory is volatile (forgets when power is off)?
questions.why: RAM loses its contents without power.

questions.q: Which layer is the structural skeleton that also often works as the antenna?
questions.why: Metal frames are split by plastic bands into antenna sections.

questions.q: What usually makes most scratches on cover glass?
options: Sand (quartz), which is harder than glass
questions.why: Quartz particles in dust and sand are harder than glass.

questions.q: Why are OLED blacks so deep?
options: Black pixels are simply switched off
questions.why: Self-emissive pixels emit no light when off.

options: A damaged lithium cell heating itself until it may catch fire
questions.why: It is why batteries must never be punctured.

questions.q: Which change would most help a phone with too little RAM that stutters with many apps open?
options: More RAM / a phone with more RAM
questions.why: Running apps live in RAM; storage size does not fix that.

questions.q: During a battery replacement, which order is correct?
options: Disconnect the battery → replace → test → seal

questions.q: Why is RAM stacked on top of the SoC (package-on-package)?
options: Shorter connections allow higher speed and lower power
questions.why: Short wires reduce delay and energy per bit.

courses.title: Inside a PC — build one
courses.summary: Meet every part of a desktop PC in 3D, learn the real build order, practise a hardware-technician interview and plan your own build.
outcomes: Learners can identify the main parts of a desktop PC and what each does
Learners can describe the correct order to assemble a PC
Learners can explain basic power, display and cooling troubleshooting
Learners can answer common desktop-support interview questions clearly

scenes.text: Kabir has saved for months to build a gaming PC. The boxes arrive — but which part does what?
His cousin, an IT technician, opens the 3D model: "Let's meet each part before we touch anything."

steps.title: Seven key parts
steps.body: A desktop PC needs: **CPU** (does the thinking), **motherboard** (connects everything), **RAM** (working memory), **storage** (SSD), **power supply** (PSU), **cooling** and a **case**. A **graphics card** (GPU) is needed for gaming and 3D work, unless the CPU has integrated graphics.

steps.title: Everything plugs into the motherboard
steps.body: CPU into the socket, RAM into DIMM slots, the SSD into an M.2 slot, the GPU into the top PCIe x16 slot, and cables from the PSU to the board (24-pin and 8-pin CPU) and to the GPU.

steps.title: Static safety
steps.body: Before touching parts, unplug the PC and touch bare metal of the case (or wear an anti-static wrist strap) so a static spark does not damage chips.

activity.prompt: Explode the PC and tap each part you are asked to find.

tasks.goal: Find the board everything plugs into
Find the part that converts mains AC to DC

quiz.q: Which part converts mains electricity (230 V AC in India) to low-voltage DC?
quiz.why: The PSU outputs 12 V, 5 V and 3.3 V DC.

quiz.q: Where does the graphics card usually go?
quiz.why: The top x16 slot is wired to the CPU's PCIe lanes.
RAM holds the data programs are using right now.

quiz.q: Why touch bare metal on the case before handling parts?

scenes.text: Kabir's friend installed the motherboard first and then could not reach the CPU cooler's back-plate.
Order matters: some steps are much easier on the desk than inside the case.

steps.title: A proven order
steps.body: 1) CPU into the socket on the desk  2) thermal paste + cooler  3) RAM  4) M.2 SSD  5) motherboard into the case on standoffs  6) PSU and main cables  7) GPU and its power  8) fans, front-panel and storage cables  9) first boot into BIOS/UEFI.

steps.title: Thermal paste
steps.body: Apply a small pea-sized dot in the middle of the CPU and let the cooler's pressure spread it. Too much is messy; too little leaves air gaps.

steps.title: Check before you power on
steps.body: Look for loose screws, unconnected CPU power (8-pin EPS) and the GPU power cable — the most common reasons a new build will not start or show a picture.

activity.prompt: Take the guided tour (🧭) to follow the real build order, then find the parts below.

quiz.q: Why install the CPU and cooler before putting the motherboard in the case?
options: There is more room and support on the desk
quiz.why: Working on the desk is easier and safer for the socket.

quiz.q: How much thermal paste is usually enough?
quiz.why: Mounting pressure spreads a small dot evenly.

quiz.q: Which cable, if forgotten, commonly stops a new PC from booting?
options: The USB cable for a mouse
quiz.why: The CPU needs its own power connector.

quiz.q: What should you do on the first boot?
options: Enter the BIOS/UEFI and check every part is detected
quiz.why: Confirm CPU, RAM and drives are recognised before installing the OS.

lessons.title: Lab: Mock interview — desktop support technician

scenes.text: Meena has an interview for a desktop-support role tomorrow. She knows the hardware but freezes when asked to explain it.
Her mentor says: "Practise out loud. Interviewers listen for your order of checks, safety and how you confirm the fix."

steps.title: Structure your answers
steps.body: For troubleshooting questions use: **simple checks first → isolate the fault → fix → verify → document**. For behaviour questions use STAR: **Situation, Task, Action, Result**.

steps.title: Say it, then type it
steps.body: Answer aloud first, then type or dictate. The key-point check is simple word matching — use the real names of parts and steps.

steps.title: What interviewers really check
steps.body: Safety (power off, ESD), customer communication, and whether you would escalate when stuck. Saying "I would log it in the ticket" shows you understand teamwork.

tips: Think aloud: interviewers want to hear your troubleshooting order.
Start with the simplest, safest checks (power, cables) before opening hardware.
Mention safety (ESD, mains power) and backing up data — it shows maturity.
Close each answer with how you would confirm the fix worked.

rounds.q: A user's desktop shows no signs of life when the power button is pressed. Walk me through your troubleshooting.
points: check the wall socket, power cable and PSU switch
test with a known-good outlet or power cable
check the front-panel power switch connection
test or swap the power supply
reseat the 24-pin and CPU power connectors
rounds.model: I would start outside the case: confirm the socket works, the power cable is firmly in, and the PSU's rear switch is on. Then I would try a known-good cable and outlet. If still dead, I would open the case (power off, unplugged, ESD strap), check that the 24-pin and 8-pin CPU connectors are seated and that the front-panel power-switch header is on the right pins. Next I would test the PSU with a tester or swap in a known-good one. If the PSU is fine, I would strip the system down to the minimum (board, CPU, one RAM stick) to isolate a faulty component, and I would log every step in the ticket.
followups: How would you tell a dead PSU from a dead motherboard?
What does a motherboard's standby LED tell you?

rounds.q: The PC powers on, fans spin, but there is no display and it beeps. What does that suggest and what do you do?
points: beep codes or POST LEDs point to the failing component
reseat RAM or test one stick at a time
check the monitor input and cable
reseat or test the graphics card
look up the board manual for the code
rounds.model: Beeps or debug LEDs are the motherboard's POST telling me what failed, so I would look up the code in the board's manual — often it means memory or graphics. First I would rule out the simple things: monitor on, right input, cable plugged into the graphics card rather than the motherboard output. Then I would reseat the RAM, try one stick in the recommended slot, and reseat the GPU and its power cable. If a single component makes the difference, that is the faulty part.
followups: Why should the monitor be plugged into the GPU and not the motherboard?
What is POST?

rounds.q: A user says their PC is very slow and hot, and the fan is loud. What could be wrong?
points: dust blocking the heatsink, filters and fans
dried thermal paste on the CPU
background processes or malware using the CPU
check fan curves and airflow direction
rounds.model: Loud fans and heat usually mean poor cooling or a busy CPU. I would first check Task Manager for processes using the CPU — malware or a stuck update can cause it. Then I would read temperatures with a monitoring tool. If temperatures are high at light load, I would power down and clean the dust from the filters, heatsink fins and fans, check that the fans blow in the right directions, and if the PC is old, replace dried thermal paste. Finally I would re-test temperatures under load to confirm.
followups: What is thermal throttling?
How much thermal paste is the right amount?

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you had to explain a technical problem to someone who was not technical.
points: describe the situation and who the person was
avoid jargon and use an analogy
share the result and what you learned
rounds.model: In my college lab a professor's laptop kept losing Wi-Fi before lectures. The situation was stressful because he had a class in ten minutes. I explained, without jargon, that the laptop was falling asleep to save power and dropping the connection, like a phone that locks itself. I showed him the one setting to change, asked him to try it himself so I knew he understood, and followed up the next day. The result was no more drops — and I learned that a simple analogy plus letting the person do it builds trust.
followups: What would you do if the person became angry?

rounds.q: Why do you want to work in desktop support, and where do you see yourself in two years?
points: genuine interest in fixing problems and helping people
link growth to the team's needs
rounds.model: I enjoy solving practical problems and helping people get back to work — that is exactly what desktop support does every day. I already build and repair PCs, and I am comfortable with Windows troubleshooting and basic networking. In two years I would like to have grown into L2 support, ideally with a recognised certification, and to be the person on the team who documents fixes well so others can reuse them.
followups: Which certification would you aim for first, and why?

quiz.q: In STAR answers, what does the R stand for?
What should a troubleshooting answer end with?
options: How you verified the fix and documented it
quiz.why: Verification and documentation close the loop.

quiz.q: A PC beeps and shows no picture. What is a sensible first step?
options: Look up the beep/POST code and check RAM and display cable
quiz.why: POST codes point to the failing component.

quiz.q: Why mention safety in a hardware interview?
options: It shows you work without damaging equipment or hurting yourself
quiz.why: Safe working is a basic requirement.

lessons.title: Capstone lab: Assemble the build in order

scenes.text: All parts are on the table. Kabir has 2 hours and wants it to boot first time.
He writes the order on a sticky note before he opens a single box.

steps.title: Plan, then build
steps.body: Check compatibility first: CPU socket matches the motherboard, RAM type (DDR4 vs DDR5) matches the board, the PSU has enough wattage and the right connectors, and the GPU fits the case.

steps.title: A quick power budget
steps.body: CPU 120 W + GPU 220 W + rest ~80 W ≈ 420 W. A good-quality 650 W PSU leaves comfortable headroom.

steps.title: Keep the manual open
steps.body: The motherboard manual shows which RAM slots to use and how the tiny front-panel pins are wired.

activity.prompt: Put these PC build steps in the correct order.
items: Check compatibility: CPU socket, RAM type, PSU wattage, case size
Install the CPU in the motherboard socket on the desk
Apply thermal paste and mount the CPU cooler
Install RAM in the recommended slots
Install the M.2 SSD
Mount the motherboard on the case standoffs
Install the PSU and connect the 24-pin and 8-pin CPU cables
Install the graphics card and connect its power
Connect fans and front-panel headers
Power on, enter BIOS/UEFI and check every part is detected

quiz.q: What must match between the CPU and the motherboard?
quiz.why: A CPU only fits and works in its own socket type.

quiz.q: DDR5 RAM in a DDR4-only motherboard will…

quiz.why: The notch position differs between DDR generations.

quiz.q: Roughly what PSU suits a build drawing about 420 W?
quiz.why: Headroom keeps the PSU efficient and quiet.

quiz.q: Where do you find which RAM slots to use for dual channel?
quiz.why: Boards differ; the manual tells you.

questions.q: Where does an M.2 NVMe SSD connect?

questions.why: M.2 slots carry PCIe lanes for NVMe drives.

questions.q: What does the PSU's 24-pin cable connect to?
questions.why: It is the main ATX power connector.

questions.q: What is the purpose of thermal paste?
options: Fill microscopic air gaps between CPU and cooler
Make the CPU faster by itself

questions.why: Front intake, rear/top exhaust is the common layout.

questions.q: A new build powers on but shows no picture; the monitor is plugged into the motherboard while a GPU is installed. Most likely fix?
options: Plug the monitor into the graphics card
questions.why: With a discrete GPU the display output is on the card.

questions.q: Why is the CPU usually installed before the motherboard goes into the case?
options: It is easier and safer to work on the desk
questions.why: More space and support for the socket.

options: An AM5 CPU in an AM5 motherboard
A GPU in an M.2 slot
A 2.5-inch drive in a DIMM slot
DDR5 RAM in a DDR4 slot

questions.q: A PC is hot and loud at idle. What is the best order of checks?
options: Check CPU usage → read temperatures → clean dust/check fans → refresh thermal paste → retest
questions.why: Cheap, safe checks first, then verify.

courses.title: How a chip is made (wafer → package)
courses.summary: Follow a computer chip from a silicon wafer to a finished package: read a wafer map, look inside a FinFET transistor, then see how the die is packaged and cooled.
outcomes: Learners can explain what a wafer, a die and yield are
Learners can describe the parts of a FinFET and why the gate wraps the fin
Learners can explain the layers of a flip-chip package and the heat path
Learners can order the main steps of chip manufacturing

scenes.text: In a chip factory (a fab), Priya's team finishes a batch of 300 mm wafers after about three months of processing.
Each wafer is probed. The red dies failed. "Our yield decides whether this product makes money," says her manager.

steps.title: Wafer, die, yield
steps.body: A **wafer** is a thin disc of single-crystal silicon. Hundreds of identical **dies** (chips) are built on it at once. After testing, **yield = good dies ÷ total dies**.

steps.title: Why big chips cost more
steps.body: If random defects land at the same rate per area, a bigger die is more likely to contain one — and fewer big dies fit on a round wafer, with more wasted at the edge.

steps.title: Lithography fields
steps.body: A scanner prints one exposure field at a time — at most 26 × 33 mm — and steps across the wafer, so very large dies must fit inside one field (or be split into chiplets).

activity.prompt: Explore the wafer map. Find each feature and read what it means.

tasks.goal: Find a die that failed wafer sort

quiz.why: Each square on the wafer is one die.

quiz.q: A wafer has 400 complete dies and 360 pass testing. What is the yield?

options: They run off the round edge and are incomplete
quiz.why: Square dies cannot fill a circle perfectly.
Machines use it to align every wafer the same way.

scenes.text: As transistors shrank, flat (planar) ones started leaking current even when switched off, wasting power and heating chips.
Engineers stood the channel up as a thin fin and wrapped the gate around it.

steps.title: A transistor is a switch
steps.body: Current flows from **source** to **drain** through a **channel**. The **gate**, separated by an ultra-thin insulator, controls the channel with its electric field — on or off.

steps.title: Why wrap the gate?
steps.body: In a FinFET the gate covers the top and both sides of the fin, so it controls the channel from three sides. Better control means less leakage when off. The newest processes go further with gate-all-around nanosheets.

steps.title: A short history
steps.body: FinFETs entered volume production around the 22 nm generation (2011–2012). Gate-all-around designs arrived at the leading-edge nodes in the 2020s.

activity.prompt: Explode the FinFET and identify its parts.

tasks.goal: Find the gate that wraps three sides

quiz.q: What controls whether a transistor is on?
quiz.why: The gate's field forms or removes the channel.

quiz.q: Why does a FinFET leak less than a planar transistor at small sizes?
options: The gate controls the channel from three sides
quiz.why: More gate control = better switching off.

quiz.q: What is the high-k dielectric for?
options: Insulating the gate from the channel while allowing strong control
quiz.why: High-k films insulate with less leakage than very thin SiO₂.

quiz.q: Which design wraps the gate fully around the channel?
quiz.why: GAA surrounds the channel on all sides.

scenes.text: A laptop chip makes tens of watts of heat in an area smaller than a postage stamp.
The package must connect thousands of signals AND move that heat out.

steps.title: Flip-chip layers
steps.body: The die is flipped face-down onto tiny **bumps** on a **package substrate**, protected by **underfill**. The substrate fans out to **solder balls** (BGA) on the motherboard. A **lid** (heat spreader) sits on top with thermal material in between.

steps.title: The heat path
steps.body: Transistors → silicon → TIM1 → heat spreader → thermal paste (TIM2) → heatsink → air. Every interface adds resistance, which is why paste quality and mounting pressure matter.

steps.title: Why flip-chip?
steps.body: Bumps can cover the whole die area, giving thousands of short connections — far more than wire bonds around the edge.

activity.prompt: Explode the package and follow both the electrical path and the heat path.

tasks.goal: Find the bumps joining die and substrate
Find the solder balls that attach to the motherboard

quiz.q: In flip-chip packaging, the die's transistor side faces…
quiz.why: The active side faces the bumps.

quiz.q: What does the package substrate do?
options: Fans out tiny die connections to the larger ball pitch of a PCB
quiz.why: It re-routes fine-pitch bumps to board-friendly balls.

options: Sharing thermal-expansion stress around the bumps
quiz.why: It protects the bumps from cracking.

quiz.q: Which order is the heat path?
options: Die → TIM → lid → paste → heatsink → air
quiz.why: Heat flows out through each layer to the air.

lessons.title: Capstone lab: Put the fab flow in order

scenes.text: A visitor asks: "How do you turn sand into a phone chip?"
The tour guide draws the whole journey on a whiteboard — it takes months and hundreds of steps.

steps.title: Front end and back end
steps.body: **Front end of line**: build transistors with repeated cycles of deposition, photolithography, etching and doping. **Back end of line**: stack many copper wiring layers above them.

steps.title: Why so many steps?
steps.body: Each layer needs its own pattern. A modern chip can go through dozens of lithography exposures, so one wafer may take around three months to finish.

steps.title: Global supply chain
steps.body: Sand becomes silicon in one country, wafers are processed in another, and packaging and testing often happen in a third — which is why chip shortages affect everyone.

activity.prompt: Order the main steps of making a chip.
items: Purify silicon and grow a single-crystal ingot
Slice the ingot into wafers and polish them
Build transistors: deposit, pattern (lithography), etch and dope — many times
Add the metal interconnect layers
Test every die on the wafer (wafer sort)
Dice the wafer into individual dies
Package the good dies (bumps, substrate, underfill, lid)
Final test and ship

options: Every die is probed electrically before dicing

quiz.q: Which process transfers a pattern onto the wafer?
quiz.why: Light through a mask exposes a resist pattern.

quiz.q: When are metal wiring layers added?
options: After the transistors are built (back end of line)

quiz.q: Why test before dicing and packaging?
options: It is cheaper not to package bad dies
quiz.why: Packaging a bad die wastes money.

questions.q: What material are most computer chips built on?

questions.why: The fraction of dies that work.

questions.q: Which part of a transistor controls the channel?
questions.why: The gate's voltage turns it on or off.

questions.q: Approximately how thick is a 300 mm wafer?
What connects a flip-chip die to the package substrate?
questions.why: Thousands of bumps across the die area.

questions.q: Why do FinFETs have lower leakage than planar transistors at small sizes?
options: The gate wraps three sides of the fin

questions.q: Which step comes immediately after building the transistors?
A wafer has 500 complete dies; 425 pass. If defects double, which is most likely?
Why do large dies waste more silicon at the wafer edge?
options: Fewer large squares fit inside a circle, leaving more unusable area
questions.why: Packing squares into a circle loses more area with bigger squares.

questions.q: In a flip-chip CPU, what is the role of the integrated heat spreader?
options: Spread the die's heat over a larger area and protect it
questions.why: It moves heat to the cooler and shields the die.

courses.title: Seeing 4D to 8D: hypercubes
courses.summary: Nobody can see a fourth spatial dimension — but we can compute exact shadows and slices of 4D to 8D shapes. Rotate a tesseract, slice it, count its faces, and connect it to high-dimensional data.
outcomes: Learners can explain what a dimension is in coordinates
Learners can count vertices and edges of an n-cube and n-simplex
Learners can describe projection and slicing as two honest ways to view higher dimensions
Learners can relate n-dimensional geometry to datasets with many features

scenes.text: Imagine a flat creature living on a sheet of paper. A cube passing through its world looks like a square that appears, stays, and vanishes.
We are in the same position with a 4D cube: we can only see its 3D shadow or 3D slices.

steps.title: Dimensions are coordinates
steps.body: A point on a line needs 1 number, on a plane 2, in space 3. A **4D** point simply needs 4 numbers (x, y, z, w). Mathematics works the same way in 8 dimensions — it is just harder to picture.

steps.title: Build cubes by doubling
steps.body: Take a point, slide it → a segment (2 vertices). Slide the segment → a square (4). Slide the square → a cube (8). Slide the cube in a 4th direction → a **tesseract** with **16 vertices and 32 edges**. An n-cube has **2ⁿ vertices** and **n·2ⁿ⁻¹ edges**.

steps.title: What you are really seeing
steps.body: The model is a **projection** (a shadow). Edges that look bent or cubes that look squashed are artefacts of projecting — in 4D every edge is the same length and every corner is a right angle. A rotation always turns a **plane** (like X–W), not around an axis.

activity.prompt: Rotate the tesseract in the X–W and Y–W planes, then switch dimensions and watch how the shadow changes. Turn on slice mode at 4D.

quiz.q: How many vertices does a 4D hypercube (tesseract) have?
How many edges does a tesseract have?
What does a rotation in the X–W plane change?
options: The x and w coordinates, leaving y and z alone

quiz.q: Why do some edges look shorter in the 3D shadow?
quiz.why: All edges of an n-cube are equal; the shadow distorts them.

scenes.text: A triangle's 3 corners are all connected. A tetrahedron's 4 corners are all connected.
Keep going: a 5D simplex has 6 corners, each joined to every other — 15 edges.

steps.title: The simplex family
steps.body: A **simplex** is the simplest shape in each dimension: point, segment, triangle, tetrahedron, then the 4-simplex (5 vertices), 5-simplex (6 vertices)… An n-simplex has **n+1 vertices** and every pair is joined, so it has **n(n+1)/2 edges**.

steps.title: Counting faces
steps.body: The number of m-dimensional faces of an n-simplex is C(n+1, m+1). For the 4-simplex: 5 vertices, 10 edges, 10 triangles, 5 tetrahedra.

steps.title: Where this appears
steps.body: Simplices describe mixtures and probabilities: three percentages that add to 100% live on a triangle; five that add to 100% live on a 4-simplex.

activity.prompt: Explore the 5-simplex: rotate it in planes that use V and W, change the dimension and compare perspective with orthographic projection.

quiz.q: How many vertices does a 5-simplex have?
How many edges does a 4-simplex have?
In orthographic projection, extra coordinates are…
quiz.why: Orthographic projection drops the axis without perspective.

quiz.q: Three proportions that add up to 1 can be drawn as points in…

lessons.title: Capstone lab: Count faces up to 8D

scenes.text: Anaya's dataset has 8 features per student: marks, attendance, sleep… Each student is a point in 8D space.
She cannot see 8D — so she uses projection (like PCA) to look at 2D shadows, knowing information is lost.

steps.title: The n-cube face formula
steps.body: An n-cube has C(n, m)·2ⁿ⁻ᵐ faces of dimension m. For m = 1 (edges) that is n·2ⁿ⁻¹.

steps.title: Worked example: the 5-cube
steps.body: Vertices 2⁵ = 32. Edges 5·2⁴ = 80. Squares C(5,2)·2³ = 80. Cubes C(5,3)·2² = 40. Tesseracts C(5,4)·2 = 10.

steps.title: Check with the model
steps.body: Open the hypercube lesson again and switch dimensions — the table beside the model shows the same counts.

activity.prompt: How many edges does a 6-dimensional cube have? (Use n·2ⁿ⁻¹.)

quiz.q: How many vertices does an 8-cube have?
How many edges does a 5-cube have?
A dataset with 8 numeric features per row lives in…
What does PCA do, in this picture?
options: Projects high-dimensional data to fewer dimensions, losing some information
quiz.why: Like the shadow of a hypercube.

questions.q: How many numbers are needed to locate a point in 4D space?
How many vertices does a cube (3-cube) have?
How many edges does a tesseract have?

options: In a plane such as X–W

questions.q: How many vertices does a 4-simplex have?
Slicing an axis-aligned tesseract with the hyperplane w = 0 gives…
questions.why: Like slicing a cube with z = 0 gives a square.

questions.q: How many squares (2-faces) does a tesseract have?
How many 3-cube cells bound a tesseract?
How many edges does an 8-cube have?
Which statement about the 3D shadow of a hypercube is honest?
options: It is what a 4D being sees
It is an exact projection that distorts lengths and angles
questions.why: Projection preserves structure but not lengths.

courses.title: Qubits on the Bloch sphere
courses.summary: A qubit's state is an arrow on a sphere. Drag it, apply X, H, S and T gates, measure it, and learn exactly how the angles set the odds of reading 0 or 1.
outcomes: Learners can describe a qubit state with angles θ and φ
Learners can compute measurement probabilities P(0) = cos²(θ/2)
Learners can predict the effect of X, Z, H and S gates on the sphere
Learners can explain what measurement does to a qubit

scenes.text: A normal bit is like a coin lying heads or tails: 0 or 1.
A qubit is more like an arrow that can point anywhere on a globe — but when you measure it, you only ever get 0 or 1.

steps.title: The Bloch sphere
steps.body: Every pure qubit state can be written |ψ⟩ = cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + e^(iφ)·sin(θ/2)|1⟩. The angle **θ** is measured from the north pole |0⟩; **φ** is the angle around the equator (the relative phase).

steps.title: Probabilities
steps.body: Measuring gives 0 with probability **P(0) = cos²(θ/2)** and 1 with **P(1) = sin²(θ/2)**. At the equator (θ = 90°) both are 50%.

steps.title: Try the gates
steps.body: **X** flips |0⟩ ↔ |1⟩ (180° about X). **H** turns |0⟩ into |+⟩ on the equator. **S** and **T** rotate around Z by 90° and 45°, changing only the phase φ.

activity.prompt: Drag the orange state arrow (or use the θ/φ sliders and gates) to complete the four goals.

quiz.q: Where is the state |0⟩ on the Bloch sphere?
What is P(1) for a state on the equator?
What does the X gate do to |0⟩?
Which angle changes only the phase, not the measurement odds?
quiz.why: φ is the relative phase; P(0) depends only on θ.

scenes.text: Quantum programmers talk about |0⟩, |1⟩, |+⟩, |−⟩, |+i⟩ and |−i⟩ all the time.
On the Bloch sphere they are just the six ends of the X, Y and Z axes.

steps.title: The six axis states
steps.body: |0⟩ and |1⟩ are the poles (Z axis). |+⟩ and |−⟩ are the X-axis ends: (|0⟩ ± |1⟩)/√2. |+i⟩ and |−i⟩ are the Y-axis ends: (|0⟩ ± i|1⟩)/√2.

steps.title: Same odds, different states
steps.body: |+⟩ and |−⟩ both give 50/50 when measured, yet they are opposite points: the minus sign (phase) matters in interference. H turns |+⟩ back into |0⟩ but |−⟩ into |1⟩.

steps.title: Opposite = distinguishable
steps.body: Any two opposite points on the sphere are orthogonal states: a suitable measurement can tell them apart perfectly.

activity.prompt: Tap each named state on the sphere and read its formula.

quiz.q: Which axis do |+⟩ and |−⟩ lie on?

quiz.why: Like |+⟩, it is on the equator.

scenes.text: A lab prepares a qubit tilted θ = 60° from the north pole.
They prepare and measure it 1,000 times. About how many 0s should they see?

steps.title: Many shots
steps.body: One measurement gives a single 0 or 1. Only by repeating the same preparation many times do the frequencies approach the probabilities — about 750 zeros out of 1,000 here.

steps.title: Measurement changes the state
steps.body: After a measurement the qubit collapses to |0⟩ or |1⟩. You cannot measure the same copy again to learn θ.

activity.prompt: A qubit has θ = 60°. What is the probability (in %) of measuring 0?

quiz.q: For θ = 90°, out of 1,000 measurements you expect about…
For θ = 120°, which is closest to P(0)?

questions.q: The north pole of the Bloch sphere is…
What does the H gate do to |0⟩?
P(0) for a qubit is given by…
The S gate rotates the state about Z by…
What does the Z gate do to |+⟩?
questions.why: A 180° turn about Z swaps |+⟩ and |−⟩.

questions.q: Which pair gives identical measurement odds in the 0/1 basis but are different states?
Why do experiments repeat the same preparation thousands of times?
options: One measurement gives only one 0 or 1; frequencies estimate the probabilities

questions.q: Starting at |0⟩, apply H then S. Where is the state?
questions.why: H gives |+⟩; S rotates |+⟩ by 90° about Z to |+i⟩.

tech-security-devops.title: Cybersecurity and DevOps
tech-security-devops.description: Protect people and systems — the CIA triad, threats, phishing, cryptography, OWASP Top 10 and Security+-style operations — and ship software safely with CI/CD, containers, Kubernetes and infrastructure as code.

courses.title: Cybersecurity foundations for everyone
courses.summary: The core ideas of security in plain language: the CIA triad, common threats and malware, phishing and scams (with India's reporting options), passwords and multi-factor authentication, and the cryptography that protects everyday life. Topic tags show which syllabus this can support. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can explain confidentiality, integrity, availability and AAA with examples
Learners can recognise common malware and social-engineering attacks
Learners can spot phishing and UPI/OTP scams and know how to report cybercrime in India
Learners can explain hashing, symmetric and asymmetric encryption, digital signatures and TLS

lessons.title: The CIA triad: what security protects

scenes.text: At a school in Ranchi, a spreadsheet of Class 10 pre-board marks was accidentally shared to a public link. Parents saw other children's marks.
Days later, someone with the link quietly changed a few marks. Then the school's website went down on results day under heavy traffic.
The computer teacher, Mr. Minz, used it to teach his class: 'Three different failures. Confidentiality broken by the leak, integrity broken by the edits, availability broken by the outage.'

steps.title: Confidentiality, integrity, availability
steps.body:
- **Confidentiality:** only the right people can see information. Tools: access control, encryption, classification ('internal', 'confidential').
- **Integrity:** information is accurate and not changed without authorisation. Tools: permissions, hashing, digital signatures, version history, audit logs.
- **Availability:** systems and data are there when needed. Tools: backups, redundancy, capacity planning, DDoS protection, patching.
Most security decisions balance these three. Locking a file so tightly that doctors cannot open it in an emergency protects confidentiality but harms availability.

steps.title: AAA and non-repudiation
steps.body:
- **Authentication:** proving who you are (password, OTP, fingerprint).
- **Authorisation:** what you are allowed to do once identified (read marks vs edit marks).
- **Accounting (auditing):** recording who did what and when (logs).
- **Non-repudiation:** someone cannot credibly deny an action they took — e.g. a digitally signed document.

steps.title: Risk in one line
steps.body:
**Risk ≈ likelihood × impact.** A threat (someone or something that could cause harm) exploits a vulnerability (a weakness) to damage an asset (something of value).
Responses to a risk: **mitigate** (add controls), **transfer** (insurance, outsourcing), **avoid** (stop the risky activity), **accept** (consciously live with it).

steps.title: Worked example: fixing the school's problems
steps.body:
- Confidentiality: share marks only with named staff accounts, never 'anyone with the link'; parents see only their own child's marks through a login.
- Integrity: only the exam cell can edit; keep version history; log every change.
- Availability: host results on a service that can scale; publish a backup PDF link; test with expected traffic beforehand.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Think of your phone. Write one threat to each of its confidentiality, integrity and availability, and one control you already use (or should) for each.

activity.prompt: Which part of the CIA triad was mainly harmed?

items.text: A hacker reads customers' Aadhaar-linked records
Someone edits bank account numbers in invoices
An email with salary data goes to the wrong person
A website crashes during a flash sale
Exam marks are changed without permission

quiz.why: Encryption protects confidentiality: only someone with the key can read the data.
Backups mainly protect availability, because you can restore data after loss. They also help recover integrity after damage.

quiz.q: Checking what a logged-in user may do is…
quiz.why: Checking what a logged-in user is allowed to do is authorisation. Authentication is proving who they are.

quiz.q: Buying cyber insurance is an example of risk…
quiz.why: Buying cyber insurance shifts the financial impact to the insurer, which is risk transfer.

quiz.q: Logs that record who changed a mark support…
quiz.why: Logs that record who changed a mark support accounting (auditing), because actions can be traced to a person.

scenes.text: Accountant Manoj in a Kanpur textile firm received a WhatsApp message: 'Your courier is on hold. Download the delivery form.' The file was named Delivery_Form.apk.
He installed it. The app asked for SMS permission. Within hours, OTPs were being read and small amounts drained from linked wallets.
The firm's IT person, Fatima, wiped the phone, reset passwords and helped him report it. Then she trained the whole office: unexpected files, urgency and requests for permissions are red flags.

steps.title: Malware types
steps.body:
- **Virus:** attaches to files/programs and spreads when they run.
- **Worm:** spreads by itself across networks, without user action.
- **Trojan:** looks legitimate (a 'delivery form' app) but hides malicious functions.
- **Ransomware:** encrypts or steals data and demands payment.
- **Spyware / keylogger:** secretly collects information or keystrokes.
- **Rootkit:** hides deep in the system to keep privileged access.
- **Botnet:** many infected devices controlled remotely, e.g. for DDoS attacks or spam.
- **Fileless malware:** runs in memory or abuses legitimate tools, leaving fewer traces.

steps.title: Social engineering
steps.body:
Attackers manipulate people rather than machines, using **urgency, fear, authority, curiosity or greed**.
- **Phishing** (email), **smishing** (SMS), **vishing** (voice calls), plus messaging apps.
- **Spear phishing:** targeted at a specific person using personal details; **whaling:** targets senior executives.
- **Pretexting:** an invented story ('I'm from your bank's KYC team').
- **Baiting:** a free USB drive or a 'free movie' download.
- **Tailgating/piggybacking:** following someone through a secure door.
- **Business email compromise:** fake or hijacked email from a 'vendor' changing bank details.

steps.title: Other common attacks
steps.body:
- **Denial of service (DoS/DDoS):** overwhelm a service so real users can't reach it.
- **Man-in-the-middle / on-path:** intercepting traffic, e.g. on fake Wi-Fi.
- **Credential stuffing:** using leaked passwords from one site on others.
- **Brute force / password spraying:** guessing many passwords, or one common password across many accounts.
- **Supply-chain attacks:** compromising software or vendors that many organisations trust.
- **Zero-day:** exploiting a vulnerability before a fix exists.

steps.title: Everyday defences
steps.body:
- Install apps only from official stores; be wary of APK files sent in chats.
- Keep OS and apps updated; enable automatic updates.
- Use a password manager and **unique** passwords; turn on MFA.
- Back up important data (with one copy offline) — the best answer to ransomware.
- Pause before acting on urgent messages; verify through an official number or app.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Check which apps on your phone have SMS, accessibility or 'display over other apps' permissions. Remove any you don't trust — these permissions are commonly abused by banking trojans.

activity.prompt: Match each attack to its description.
pairs: Following someone through a secure door
Reusing leaked passwords on other sites

quiz.q: Malware that spreads without any user action is a…
quiz.why: A worm spreads on its own across networks, without needing any user action. A virus usually needs a user to run something.

quiz.q: A targeted email to the CFO using details from LinkedIn is…
quiz.why: A targeted email to a senior executive such as the CFO, using personal details, is whaling or spear phishing.

quiz.q: Best defence against ransomware destroying your data?
options: Tested backups including an offline copy
quiz.why: The best defence against ransomware is tested backups, including an offline copy, so you can restore without paying.

quiz.q: Attackers try 'Password@123' on thousands of accounts. This is…
quiz.why: Password spraying tries one common password on many accounts. It avoids lockouts that trying many passwords on one account would cause.

quiz.q: Which emotion do social engineers most often exploit?
quiz.why: Social engineers use urgency and fear, because pressure short-circuits careful thinking.

lessons.title: Phishing, scams and what to do if it happens

scenes.text: Retired teacher Mrs. Shanta in Mysuru got a call: 'Your bank KYC expires today. Your account will be blocked. Tell me the OTP we just sent to verify.'
She remembered her granddaughter Riya's rule: 'No genuine bank asks for your OTP, PIN or password. Ever.' She hung up.
She called the number printed on her debit card. The bank confirmed it was a scam. Riya helped her report the caller's number on the national cybercrime portal.

steps.title: How to spot phishing
steps.body:
Red flags:
- **Urgency or threats:** 'account blocked in 2 hours', 'police case filed'.
- **Requests for secrets:** OTP, UPI PIN, passwords, CVV, screen-sharing or remote-access apps.
- **Look-alike senders and links:** amaz0n-offers.co, sbi-kyc-update.in; shortened links hiding the destination.
- **Too good to be true:** lottery wins, huge discounts, work-from-home 'tasks' that pay at first, then ask for 'deposits'.
- **Unexpected attachments** or QR codes.
Hover over (or long-press) links to see the real address; when in doubt, open the official app or type the website yourself.

steps.title: UPI and payment scams in India
steps.body:
- You **never** need to enter your UPI PIN to **receive** money. A 'collect request' asking for your PIN is a payment *from* you.
- Never share OTPs or install screen-sharing apps at a stranger's request.
- Scanning a QR code is for paying, not receiving.
- 'Digital arrest' calls — fake police or officials on video calls demanding money — are a scam; genuine agencies don't arrest people over video calls or demand transfers.
- Fake customer-care numbers appear in search results and social media; get numbers only from official apps, websites or your card.

steps.title: If you've been scammed — act fast
steps.body:
- **Call 1930** (national cybercrime helpline) and report at **cybercrime.gov.in** as soon as possible — quick reporting improves the chance of freezing money in transit.
- Inform your bank through its official number; block cards/UPI if needed.
- Change passwords (starting with email), turn on MFA, log out other sessions.
- Keep evidence: screenshots, transaction IDs, numbers, links.
- For immediate danger, call **112**.
Outside India, contact your bank and your country's official cybercrime reporting channel.

steps.title: At work: business email compromise
steps.body:
A 'vendor' emails: 'Our bank details have changed, please pay the new account.' Rules that stop most losses:
- Verify any change of bank details by calling a **known** number (not one in the email).
- Two-person approval for new payees and large payments.
- Report suspicious emails with the 'report phishing' button so the security team can block them for everyone.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Teach one family member the three golden rules today: never share OTP/PIN, verify via official numbers, and report on 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in.

a.text: You receive an SMS: 'Your electricity will be disconnected tonight. Call 98xxxxxx12 immediately.' What do you do?

choices.label: Call the number in the SMS
choices.feedback: Scammers use urgent bill-disconnection messages to get you on the phone.

choices.label: Check the bill in the official app/website or call the official number on your bill
choices.feedback: Correct — verify through a channel you trust.

b.text: The 'officer' asks you to install a remote-support app to 'update your meter'. What now?

choices.label: Hang up — remote-access apps give full control of your phone
Install it to avoid disconnection
choices.feedback: This lets the scammer see your screen and OTPs.

c.text: Your bill is fully paid; the SMS was fake. You report the number on cybercrime.gov.in and warn your family group.

choices.label: Finish

d.text: Money leaves your account. What first?

choices.label: Call 1930 immediately, inform the bank, uninstall the app, change passwords
choices.feedback: Fast reporting improves the chance of recovery.

e.text: Rule learned: urgency + unknown number + requests for apps, OTPs or PINs = scam. Verify through official channels and report quickly.

quiz.q: Do you need to enter your UPI PIN to receive money?
quiz.why: You never need to enter your UPI PIN to receive money. The PIN is needed only to pay, so a request asking for it is a scam.

quiz.q: India's national cybercrime helpline number is…
quiz.why: India's national cybercrime helpline is 1930. You can also report at cybercrime.gov.in.

quiz.q: A 'vendor' emails new bank details. Best action?
options: Reply to the email asking if it's real
Verify by calling a known number before changing anything
quiz.why: If a vendor emails new bank details, verify by calling a known number before changing anything. Replying to the same email may reach the scammer.

quiz.q: Which link is most suspicious for a bank?
options: The URL typed from your passbook
quiz.why: 'sbi-kyc-update-now.in' is a look-alike domain that uses urgency. The bank's real address is the one from your passbook, card or official app.

quiz.q: A stranger asks you to install a screen-sharing app. Risk?
options: They can see OTPs and control your phone
quiz.why: A screen-sharing app lets a stranger see your screen, including OTPs, and control your phone. Remote access is a top scam tool.

lessons.title: Passwords, MFA and the cryptography behind the padlock

scenes.text: College student Rohit used the same password for email, a gaming site and his food app. The gaming site was breached; his password was published online.
Attackers tried it everywhere — credential stuffing. They got into his email and reset his other passwords.
His friend Ayesha helped him recover: a password manager with unique passwords, MFA with an authenticator app, and an explanation of how websites should store passwords (hashed, never in plain text).

steps.title: Strong authentication
steps.body:
- **Length beats complexity:** a passphrase like 'mango-kite-river-42-chalk' is strong and memorable.
- **Unique password per site** — use a password manager.
- **MFA (multi-factor):** combine factors — something you know (password), have (phone, security key), are (fingerprint). Authenticator apps and hardware security keys (FIDO2/passkeys) resist phishing better than SMS codes, but any MFA is far better than none.
- **Passkeys:** passwordless sign-in using cryptographic keys stored on your device; resistant to phishing.

steps.title: Hashing
steps.body:
A **hash function** turns any input into a fixed-size fingerprint (e.g. SHA-256 gives 256 bits). Same input → same hash; a tiny change → a completely different hash; you can't reverse it to get the input.
Uses: checking file integrity (compare the published hash of a download), digital signatures, and **storing passwords**.
Passwords must be stored with slow, **salted** password-hashing algorithms (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2). A **salt** is a random value per user so identical passwords get different hashes and precomputed tables don't work.

steps.title: Encryption: symmetric and asymmetric
steps.body:
- **Symmetric encryption** (e.g. AES): the same secret key encrypts and decrypts. Fast; used for bulk data. Problem: sharing the key safely.
- **Asymmetric encryption** (e.g. RSA, elliptic-curve cryptography): a **public key** (share with anyone) and a **private key** (keep secret). Data encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the private key.
- **Digital signature:** sign with your *private* key; anyone verifies with your *public* key — proves authenticity and integrity (supports non-repudiation).
- **Certificates** bind a public key to an identity (a website's domain), issued by a trusted certificate authority.

steps.title: Worked example: what happens behind the padlock (TLS)
steps.body:
When you open https://yourbank.example:
- Your browser and the server agree on TLS settings.
- The server sends its **certificate**; your browser checks it's valid for that domain and signed by a trusted authority.
- They use asymmetric cryptography (key exchange) to agree on fresh **symmetric session keys**.
- All page data is then encrypted with fast symmetric encryption and integrity-checked.
The padlock means the connection is encrypted to that domain — **not** that the site is honest. Phishing sites can have padlocks too.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing hashing (one-way) with encryption (reversible with a key).
- Storing passwords with fast hashes like plain MD5/SHA-1 or without salt.
- Thinking 'https' means 'safe site'.
- Writing your own cryptography — use well-tested libraries and standard protocols.
- Approving MFA prompts you didn't start ('MFA fatigue' attacks) — deny and change your password.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Turn on MFA for your main email account today and save the backup codes somewhere safe offline. Then check a breach-notification service your browser or password manager offers to see if your email appears in known breaches.

statements.s: Hashing is reversible if you know the key.
statements.why: Hashes are one-way; encryption uses keys.

statements.s: A salt makes identical passwords produce different stored hashes.
statements.why: Each user gets a random salt.

statements.s: A digital signature is created with the signer's private key.
The padlock icon proves a website is trustworthy.
statements.why: It proves an encrypted connection to that domain only.

statements.s: TLS uses symmetric encryption for the bulk of the data.
statements.why: Asymmetric is used to set up keys and authenticate.

statements.s: SMS OTP is the most phishing-resistant MFA method.

options: A unique long passphrase stored in a password manager, with MFA
quiz.why: The strongest choice is a unique, long passphrase stored in a password manager, with MFA. Names, birth years and phone numbers are easy to guess.

options: Salted, slow password hashing such as bcrypt or Argon2
quiz.why: Websites should store passwords with salted, slow password hashing such as bcrypt or Argon2. Plain text, Base64 or reversible encryption can be undone.
AES is symmetric encryption: the same key is used to encrypt and decrypt.

quiz.q: To verify a signed document you use the signer's…
quiz.why: A signature is made with the signer's private key and verified with the signer's public key.

quiz.q: You get an MFA prompt you didn't initiate. Do what?
options: Deny it and change your password
quiz.why: An MFA prompt you didn't start means someone may have your password. Deny it and change your password.

questions.q: The 'C' in the CIA triad stands for…
questions.why: In the CIA triad, C stands for Confidentiality: only authorised people can see the data.

questions.q: Which is an example of MFA?
questions.why: MFA uses different types of factors, such as something you know (password) and something you have (authenticator code). Two passwords are the same type.

questions.q: A fake 'bank' SMS with a link is…
questions.why: A fake bank SMS with a link is smishing (SMS phishing). Vishing is by voice call.

questions.q: What should you never share with anyone, including 'bank staff'?
questions.why: Never share your OTP or UPI PIN with anyone, including people who claim to be bank staff. No genuine bank asks for them.
A DDoS attack overwhelms a service with traffic, so it mainly targets availability.

questions.q: A program disguised as a game that steals data is a…
questions.why: A program disguised as something useful, like a game, that steals data is a Trojan.

questions.q: Why are salts used in password storage?
options: So identical passwords get different hashes and precomputed attacks fail
questions.why: A salt is random data added to each password before hashing. Identical passwords then get different hashes, and precomputed attacks fail.

questions.q: In TLS, the server's certificate mainly proves…
options: The public key belongs to that domain
questions.why: A TLS certificate proves that the public key belongs to that domain. It doesn't mean the site is honest or bug-free.
Risk is commonly estimated as likelihood × impact.

questions.q: A user's password leaked from one site is used to log in to another. This is…
questions.why: Using a password leaked from one site to log in to another is credential stuffing. It works because people reuse passwords.
