tech-semi-fab-a.description: Manufacturing deep dive part A: quartz → polysilicon → Czochralski ingot → polished wafer → cleanroom → thermal oxidation → DUV/EUV photolithography, with real fab tickets and number labs.

courses.title: From sand to silicon: quartz to 11-nines polysilicon
courses.summary: How ordinary quartz becomes the purest material humans make in bulk: carbothermic reduction to metallurgical silicon, chlorination to trichlorosilane, distillation and the Siemens process to electronic-grade polysilicon.
outcomes: Describe the chemistry from SiO₂ to metallurgical-grade silicon
Explain the Siemens process and why chlorosilanes are distilled
Convert 'nines' of purity into impurity concentrations
Distinguish metallurgical, solar and electronic grades

lessons.title: Quartz, arc furnaces and metallurgical silicon

scenes.text: People say 'chips are made from sand', but fabs start from high-purity quartz (quartzite) rock, not beach sand full of shells and iron.
In a submerged-arc furnace at around 2000 °C, carbon strips the oxygen from SiO₂.

steps.title: Carbothermic reduction
steps.body: SiO₂ + 2C → Si + 2CO (overall). Carbon comes from coal, coke and wood chips; graphite electrodes carry huge currents. Output: **metallurgical-grade silicon (MG-Si)**, ~98–99 % pure. Most MG-Si goes to aluminium alloys and silicones; a small share feeds the solar and chip chain.

steps.title: Why not stop here
steps.body: 1 % impurity is ~5×10²⁰ foreign atoms/cm³ — far more than the 10¹⁵–10¹⁶ cm⁻³ of dopant we deliberately add. Metals like iron kill carrier lifetime, so the silicon must be purified chemically.

steps.title: Energy-hungry
steps.body: Silicon smelting uses roughly 11–13 MWh per tonne, so smelters are sited near cheap power.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Zone refining or Czochralski growth alone cannot purify MG-Si to electronic grade economically; the big purification step is the gas-phase chemistry.

activity.prompt: Complete the overall reaction in the arc furnace.

lessons.title: Lab: The Siemens process in order

scenes.text: In a polysilicon plant, rods of silicon glow at ~1100 °C inside bell-jar reactors.
Trichlorosilane gas decomposes on them, growing ultrapure silicon layer by layer.

steps.title: Chemistry
steps.body:
1. Si + 3HCl → SiHCl₃ + H₂ (fluidised bed, ~300 °C).
2. Fractional distillation of SiHCl₃ (boiling point ~32 °C) removes boron, phosphorus and metal chlorides.
3. SiHCl₃ + H₂ → Si + 3HCl on heated thin silicon rods (Siemens CVD reactor).

steps.title: Output
steps.body: Electronic-grade polysilicon (EG-Si), 9N–11N pure (99.9999999 %–99.999999999 %). Rods are crushed into chunks, etched and bagged in cleanrooms.

steps.title: Alternatives
steps.body: Fluidised-bed reactors using silane (SiH₄) make granular polysilicon with less energy, mostly for solar.

Deposit silicon on heated rods with hydrogen (Siemens reactor)
Crush rods into chunks and etch the surface
Pack chunks in cleanroom bags for crystal growers

steps.title: Worked: 9N
steps.body: Impurity fraction = 10⁻⁹ (1 ppb atomic). Impurities = 5×10²² × 10⁻⁹ = **5×10¹³ cm⁻³** — already below typical substrate doping (10¹⁵).

steps.title: Worked: 6N solar
steps.body: 6N → 10⁻⁶ → 5×10¹⁶ cm⁻³. Solar cells tolerate more, but metals still reduce efficiency.

steps.title: Shortcut
steps.body: Impurity density = 5×10²² × 10⁻ᴺ for N nines.

courses.title: Czochralski crystal growth
courses.summary: Growing a perfect single crystal 300 mm wide and up to ~2 m long: seed dipping, necking (Dash neck), shoulder, body and tail; pull rate, rotation, dopant segregation and oxygen; float-zone as the alternative.
outcomes: Describe each stage of a CZ pull
Explain necking and why it removes dislocations
Apply the Scheil equation for dopant segregation
Estimate ingot mass and choose CZ vs FZ

story.title: Night shift at the crystal hall

scenes.text: Meera watches a 300 mm ingot slowly rise from glowing melt at about a millimetre per minute.
A camera watches the meniscus ring; the controller adjusts pull speed every second to hold diameter.

steps.title: Stages
steps.body:
1. Melt polysilicon + dopant in a quartz crucible under argon.
2. Dip a seed crystal; let it equilibrate.
3. **Neck**: pull a thin (~3–5 mm) fast-grown neck — dislocations grow out to the surface (Dash technique).
4. **Shoulder (crown)**: slow the pull to widen to full diameter.
5. **Body**: constant diameter for most of the length.
6. **Tail (end-cone)**: taper off to avoid thermal-shock dislocations.

steps.title: Rotation
steps.body: Seed and crucible rotate in opposite directions to homogenise the melt and control the growth interface shape.

steps.title: Oxygen
steps.body: The quartz crucible dissolves, giving CZ silicon ~10¹⁷–10¹⁸ oxygen atoms/cm³. Oxygen precipitates are useful for **intrinsic gettering** of metals but can cause defects.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Skipping or rushing the neck is a classic cause of a polycrystalline ('lost structure') ingot.

activity.prompt: Explode the Czochralski puller and tap each part.

objects.label: Puller chamber
objects.info: Water-cooled steel chamber filled with low-pressure argon.

objects.label: Quartz crucible
objects.info: Fused silica crucible holding molten silicon at ~1420 °C; it slowly dissolves, adding oxygen to the melt.

objects.label: Silicon melt
objects.info: Polysilicon chunks plus a little dopant, melted just above 1414 °C.

objects.label: Graphite heater
objects.info: Resistive graphite heater; controls the melt temperature to fractions of a degree.

objects.label: Seed crystal
objects.info: A small single crystal of known orientation (e.g. <100>) dipped into the melt.

objects.label: Growing ingot
objects.info: Pulled up at roughly 1 mm/min while rotating; diameter controlled by pull rate and temperature.

objects.label: Magnetic field (MCZ)
objects.info: Optional magnets damp melt convection for lower, more uniform oxygen.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: Radius 15 cm. Volume = π r² L = π × 225 × 100 = 70,686 cm³. Mass = 70,686 × 2.33 ≈ 164,700 g ≈ **165 kg** (body only).

steps.title: Real numbers
steps.body: Full 300 mm ingots of ~2 m weigh a few hundred kg, which is why pullers have heavy-duty seed-lift and crucibles hold hundreds of kg of polysilicon charge.

scenes.text: Wafers from the top of an n-type ingot measure higher resistivity than those from the bottom.
Because dopant prefers to stay in the melt, the melt gets richer as the crystal grows.

steps.title: Segregation coefficient
steps.body: k₀ = C_solid / C_liquid at the interface. In Si: B ≈ 0.8, P ≈ 0.35, As ≈ 0.3, Sb ≈ 0.023. k < 1 → dopant accumulates in the melt.

steps.title: Scheil equation
steps.body: C_s(f) = k₀·C₀·(1 − f)^(k₀ − 1), where f is the fraction of the melt already solidified and C₀ the initial melt concentration.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: Phosphorus, C₀ = 1×10¹⁶ cm⁻³, at f = 0.5: C_s = 0.35 × 10¹⁶ × 0.5^(−0.65) = 0.35 × 1.569 × 10¹⁶ ≈ **5.49×10¹⁵ cm⁻³**. At f = 0 it is 3.5×10¹⁵ — a 57 % rise by half-way.

steps.title: Why boron is easier
steps.body: k₀ ≈ 0.8 means p-type ingots stay much more uniform along their length.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — lost structure on the pull

scenes.text: The vision system flags facets disappearing on the ingot surface at 40 cm of body length.
You are the shift engineer.

steps.title: Signs
steps.body: A dislocation-free <100> ingot shows four straight growth ridges (facet lines). If they vanish, the crystal has gone polycrystalline or dislocated.

steps.title: Usual causes
steps.body: Particles from the crucible or chamber, melt temperature fluctuations, vibrations, too-fast pull, gas flow issues.

steps.title: Economics
steps.body: Remelting ('meltback') and re-pulling can recover polysilicon; continuing to grow wastes hours.

a.text: Growth ridges vanished at 40 cm. What first?

choices.label: Stop growth and plan a meltback
choices.feedback: Right — anything grown now is scrap.

choices.label: Keep pulling to finish the shift
choices.feedback: The rest of the ingot will be polycrystalline.

b.text: Meltback done. Before re-seeding, what do you check?

choices.label: Review the temperature and pull-rate logs and inspect for particles/crucible flakes
Re-seed immediately at a faster pull rate
choices.feedback: Repeating the same conditions risks another loss.

choices.label: Raise a maintenance ticket for the heater controller, re-seed with a proper neck, monitor closely

lessons.title: A wafer in 3D: notch, edge, flats

scenes.text: Ankit wonders why every 300 mm wafer has a tiny V-notch on its edge.

steps.title: Wafer anatomy
steps.body:
- **Diameter**: 150, 200, 300 mm (450 mm was explored but not adopted).
- **Thickness**: 300 mm wafers ≈ 775 µm; thinned to ~50–100 µm only after processing for packaging.
- **Notch** (300/200 mm) or **flats** (older 100/150 mm) mark orientation.
- **Edge exclusion**: the outer ~2–3 mm is not used for dies.
- **Laser mark**: ID on the backside or edge.

steps.title: Why thick
steps.body: A 300 mm wafer must survive robots, heating and polishing; thinner wafers would sag and break.

steps.title: Flatness
steps.body: Lithography focus depth is now tens of nanometres, so site flatness over each exposure field matters more than whole-wafer flatness.

scenes.text: The ingot is cropped, ground round, notched and then sliced by a web of diamond wire.
After lapping, etching and polishing, the surface is smoother than a mirror.

steps.title: Why each step
steps.body:
- Grinding to exact diameter + notch.
- **Diamond-wire saw**: hundreds of wafers at once; leaves saw damage.
- **Lapping/grinding**: removes saw marks, sets thickness and parallelism.
- **Edge profiling**: rounds edges to prevent chipping.
- **Etching**: removes the damaged layer.
- **Double-side polishing + final CMP**: nanometre roughness.
- **Clean + inspect**: particle scan, flatness, then pack in FOUPs/FOSBs.

steps.title: Specs
steps.body:
- **TTV** (total thickness variation): max − min thickness.
- **Bow**: deviation of the centre of the median surface.
- **Warp**: max − min of the median surface (free state).
- **SFQR/site flatness**: flatness within each exposure site — key for focus.

steps.body: Separate supplier-incoming issues from your own process (films adding stress can bow wafers).

lessons.title: Why fabs are cleaner than operating theatres

scenes.text: A human hair is ~50–100 µm across; critical features on chips are tens of nanometres.
One skin flake on a reticle could print a defect on every die.

steps.title: ISO 14644-1
steps.body: Class N limit for particles ≥ D µm per m³: **C = 10ᴺ × (0.1/D)^2.08**. ISO 5 ≈ old 'Class 100' (≤ 100 particles ≥0.5 µm per ft³). Lithography bays and tool interiors are ISO 3–4 or better.

steps.title: How
steps.body: HEPA/ULPA filters in the ceiling, vertical laminar flow, raised perforated floors, positive pressure, controlled temperature (±0.1 °C in litho) and humidity.

steps.title: Mini-environments
steps.body: Modern fabs keep wafers sealed in FOUPs (front-opening unified pods) carried by overhead hoist transport; the tool's EFEM is the cleanest zone. The open bay can then be cleaner-than-normal but not ISO 1.

steps.title: Ultrapure water
steps.body: UPW has resistivity ≈ 18.2 MΩ·cm and parts-per-trillion metals; a large fab uses millions of litres per day.

activity.prompt: Explore a cleanroom bay: filters, airflow, tool and FOUP transport.

objects.label: Perforated raised floor

objects.label: Process tool + EFEM

Order matters: top-down, clean over clean.

steps.title: Principles
steps.body: Remove outside contamination first (shoe covers, hair), then don the suit from top to bottom so clean layers cover dirty ones. Never let the suit touch the floor.

steps.title: No-nos
steps.body: No cosmetics, perfume, paper (unless cleanroom paper), pencils, or personal phones (unless approved). These shed particles or chemicals like sodium.

steps.title: Exit
steps.body: Gowns are removed in reverse and hung or sent to laundry per the fab's rules.

courses.title: Thermal oxidation & the Deal–Grove model
courses.summary: Growing SiO₂ on silicon: dry vs wet oxidation, furnace and RTP tools, the Deal–Grove linear–parabolic model, silicon consumption, oxide quality and where oxides are used today (pad oxide, STI liner, sacrificial, gate interface).
outcomes: Contrast dry and wet oxidation
Solve the Deal–Grove equation for thickness
Compute silicon consumed by oxidation
Diagnose a furnace thickness-uniformity problem

scenes.text: Tube A runs dry O₂ at 1000 °C; tube B runs steam (wet) at 1000 °C.
After an hour, tube B's oxide is several times thicker — but tube A's is denser and better quality.

steps.title: Reactions
steps.body: Dry: Si + O₂ → SiO₂. Wet: Si + 2H₂O → SiO₂ + 2H₂. Water diffuses through oxide much faster (higher solubility), so wet is much faster.

steps.title: Uses
steps.body:
- **Dry**: thin, high-quality oxides (interfacial layers, screen oxides).
- **Wet**: thick oxides (field/isolation in older LOCOS processes, masking oxides).

steps.title: Silicon consumed
steps.body: Growing thickness x of SiO₂ consumes ≈ 0.44x of silicon (densities and molecular weights). The original surface ends up ~44 % of the way into the oxide.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Oxide grows into the silicon as well as above it — so it buries the original surface.

activity.prompt: Dry or wet oxidation?

items.text: 2 nm interfacial oxide under a high-k gate

quiz.q: Which is faster at the same temperature?

scenes.text: A furnace recipe runs wet oxidation for 1 hour.
Use x² + A·x = B·(t + τ) with A = 0.11 µm, B = 0.51 µm²/h, τ = 0.

steps.title: Model
steps.body: Deal–Grove: x² + A x = B (t + τ). Thin regime (x ≪ A/2): x ≈ (B/A)(t + τ) — **linear**, reaction-limited. Thick regime: x ≈ √(B t) — **parabolic**, diffusion-limited.

steps.title: Thin dry oxides
steps.body: Deal–Grove under-predicts the fast initial growth of very thin dry oxides (< ~25 nm); τ is used to fit it.

activity.prompt: Same constants (A = 0.11 µm, B = 0.51 µm²/h, τ = 0). Thickness after 2 hours, in µm?

quiz.q: Doubling time in the parabolic regime increases x by…

lessons.title: Lab: Silicon consumed and step height

scenes.text: After oxidising a patterned wafer and stripping the oxide, a step appears in the silicon.
Compute how deep the silicon was consumed.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: Grow 300 nm oxide: Si consumed = 0.44 × 300 = 132 nm. Oxide top sits 168 nm above the original surface.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Oxidation-based isolation (LOCOS) leaves 'bird's beak' encroachment; modern processes use shallow-trench isolation (STI) with deposited oxide instead.

steps.body: Horizontal/vertical batch furnaces process 100+ wafers; temperature profile across zones must be flat (±0.5 °C). Thickness non-uniformity often traces to temperature zones, gas flow or wafer spacing.

courses.title: Photolithography: DUV, immersion & EUV
courses.summary: The most expensive step in a fab: resist coating, exposure, develop; the Rayleigh resolution and depth-of-focus formulas; DUV immersion vs EUV vs High-NA EUV; multi-patterning; overlay and OPC.
outcomes: Order the litho track sequence
Compute resolution with R = k₁λ/NA and DOF
Compare DUV immersion, EUV and High-NA EUV
Explain multi-patterning, OPC and overlay

story.title: A machine the size of a bus

scenes.text: An EUV scanner is shipped in many containers and costs well over a hundred million dollars.
It prints patterns smaller than a virus, tens of thousands of times a day.

steps.title: Optical path
steps.body: Light source → illuminator → reticle (4×) → projection optics → wafer covered in photoresist. The reticle and wafer stages scan in opposite directions with nanometre precision.

steps.title: DUV vs EUV
steps.body:
- **ArF immersion (193i)**: 193 nm, NA up to 1.35 with water, transmissive lenses.
- **EUV**: 13.5 nm, NA 0.33, all-reflective mirrors in vacuum; reflective reticles; tin-plasma source.
- **High-NA EUV**: NA 0.55, anamorphic optics, now being introduced for the most advanced nodes.

steps.title: Supplier landscape
steps.body: Leading-edge EUV scanners currently come from a single supplier; DUV scanners come from a few suppliers. Fabs plan lithography years ahead for this reason.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: 'Node name' (e.g. '3 nm') is a marketing generation label, not a feature that is literally 3 nm wide.

activity.prompt: Explode the lithography optical path from source to wafer.

objects.label: Light source
objects.info: DUV: ArF excimer laser at 193 nm. EUV: tin-droplet laser-produced plasma at 13.5 nm.

objects.label: Illuminator
objects.info: Shapes the light (dipole, quadrupole, freeform) to boost resolution.

objects.label: Reticle (mask)
objects.info: Pattern at 4× size. DUV masks are transmissive quartz-chrome; EUV masks are reflective multilayer mirrors.

objects.label: Projection optics
objects.info: Demagnifies 4×. NA sets resolution. EUV uses mirrors in vacuum because all materials absorb 13.5 nm.

objects.label: Immersion water
objects.info: ArF immersion puts water (n ≈ 1.44) between lens and wafer to reach NA 1.35.

objects.label: Wafer with resist
objects.info: Photoresist records the image; the stage scans and steps field by field.

tour.text: The source makes deep-UV or extreme-UV light.
The reticle carries the pattern at 4× size.
Projection optics shrink and focus the image.
Photoresist on the wafer records it.

steps.title: Why each bake
steps.body:
- **Prime (HMDS/adhesion)** helps resist stick.
- **Soft bake** drives out solvent.
- **Post-exposure bake (PEB)** drives acid diffusion in chemically amplified resists.
- **Hard bake** toughens resist for etch.

steps.title: BARC
steps.body: A bottom anti-reflective coating suppresses standing waves from the reflective substrate.

lessons.title: Lab: Rayleigh resolution for DUV immersion

scenes.text: R = k₁ · λ / NA. For 193 nm immersion, NA = 1.35, aggressive k₁ = 0.28.
Compute the single-exposure half-pitch.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: R = 0.28 × 193 / 1.35 ≈ **40 nm** half-pitch (~80 nm pitch). Smaller pitches need multi-patterning (LELE, SADP, SAQP) on DUV.

steps.title: Depth of focus
steps.body: DOF = k₂ · λ / NA². Higher NA improves resolution but shrinks DOF quadratically — hence flatness and leveling matter.

steps.title: k₁ tricks
steps.body: Off-axis illumination, phase-shift masks, OPC (optical proximity correction) and source–mask optimisation lower k₁ towards the physical limit of 0.25 for single exposure.

activity.prompt: Dry ArF (no water): λ = 193 nm, NA = 0.93, k₁ = 0.30. Half-pitch resolution in nm?

lessons.title: Lab: EUV and High-NA EUV resolution

scenes.text: A fab compares four DUV exposures (SAQP) against one EUV exposure for a critical metal layer.
Compute EUV single-exposure resolution.

steps.title: Trade-offs
steps.body: EUV cuts mask count and process steps, but has stochastic defects (photon shot noise), pellicle and source-power challenges. DUV multi-patterning adds steps, cost and overlay error.

steps.title: Decision factors
steps.body: Pitch, overlay budget, cost per layer (masks + passes), cycle time, tool availability, defectivity and yield ramp risk.

steps.title: Rule of thumb
steps.body: If a layer needs SAQP plus extra cut masks on DUV, a single EUV exposure often wins on cycle time and overlay — if tools and capacity are available.

tech-semi-fab-b.title: Front-end fabrication II: etch, deposition, implant, CMP, metals & 3D transistors
tech-semi-fab-b.description: Manufacturing deep dive part B: plasma and atomic-layer etch, CVD/PVD/ALD/epitaxy, ion implantation and anneals, CMP and copper interconnect, FinFET → GAA → CFET, and full CMOS integration with SPC and yield tickets.

courses.title: Etching: wet, plasma & atomic-layer
courses.summary: Transferring patterns into films: wet vs dry etch, isotropic vs anisotropic profiles, reactive-ion etching, selectivity, over-etch, end-point detection, high-aspect-ratio etch for 3D NAND, and atomic-layer etching.
outcomes: Contrast wet and dry etching and their profiles
Compute etch time with over-etch and resist budget from selectivity
Explain RIE mechanisms and end-point detection
Troubleshoot an etch-rate drift ticket

scenes.text: Old fabs dipped wafers in HF to etch oxide — fine for 5 µm lines.
At 50 nm, an isotropic etch undercuts the mask and destroys the line, so fabs moved to plasma etching.

steps.title: Wet etch
steps.body: Liquid chemistry (HF for SiO₂, hot H₃PO₄ for Si₃N₄, KOH/TMAH for Si). Highly selective, cheap, **isotropic** (except crystal-orientation-dependent Si etch). Still used for cleans and film strips.

steps.title: Dry (plasma) etch
steps.body: Reactive-ion etching (RIE): RF plasma creates radicals (chemistry) and ions accelerated by the sheath (directional bombardment). Combining both gives **anisotropic** vertical walls. Gases: fluorine (CF₄, C₄F₈) for oxide; Cl₂/HBr for silicon and metals.

steps.title: Sidewall passivation
steps.body: Polymer deposits on sidewalls protect them from lateral etch, while ions clear the bottom — the basis of deep vertical etches.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Anisotropy is not the same as selectivity: anisotropy is direction; selectivity is the rate ratio between the target film and the mask/underlayer.

activity.prompt: Wet or dry etch?

items.text: Strip a sacrificial oxide everywhere with dilute HF
Remove a silicon nitride hard mask with hot phosphoric acid
Contact holes through oxide to silicon

quiz.q: Directional bombardment in RIE comes from…
options: ions accelerated by the plasma sheath

lessons.title: Lab: Etch time and resist budget

scenes.text: You must etch 200 nm of oxide at 50 nm/min, with 20 % over-etch to clear thin spots.
Oxide:resist selectivity is 5:1. Will the resist survive?

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: Main etch = 200/50 = 4.0 min. With 20 % over-etch: 4.8 min. Resist rate = 50/5 = 10 nm/min → resist loss = 10 × 4.8 = **48 nm**.

steps.title: End-point detection
steps.body: Optical emission spectroscopy watches a plasma line (e.g. CO for oxide etch); when the film clears, the signal drops — the tool then runs a timed over-etch.

steps.title: Budget
steps.body: Starting resist thickness must exceed the loss plus a margin, or use a hard mask (SiN, TiN, amorphous carbon).

activity.prompt: Etch 300 nm of polysilicon at 120 nm/min with 25 % over-etch. Poly:resist selectivity 4:1. Resist lost (nm)?

options: film thickness and etch rate vary across the wafer

scenes.text: 3D NAND stacks well over 200 word-line layers; channel holes go several micrometres deep yet only ~100 nm wide.
Compute the aspect ratio.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: Depth 6 µm, diameter 100 nm → AR = 6000/100 = **60:1**.

steps.title: Challenges
steps.body: Aspect-ratio-dependent etching (ARDE): deeper features etch slower; ions get deflected (bowing, twisting); etch-stop on charging. Solutions: cryogenic etch, pulsed plasmas, high-power bias, splitting stacks into decks.

steps.title: Atomic-layer etching (ALE)
steps.body: Self-limiting cycles: modify the top monolayer (e.g. chlorinate), then remove only that layer with low-energy ions. Precise to ~0.1 nm per cycle, used for gate and fin trimming.

activity.prompt: A channel hole is 8 µm deep and 120 nm wide. Aspect ratio (depth ÷ width)?

quiz.q: Splitting a 3D NAND stack into decks helps because…
options: each deck needs a lower aspect ratio etch

courses.title: Thin-film deposition: CVD, PVD, ALD & epitaxy
courses.summary: How fabs build films from atoms: LPCVD, PECVD, sputtering (PVD), evaporation, atomic-layer deposition, epitaxy and electroplating; conformality, step coverage, stress and choosing the right method.
outcomes: Explain CVD, PVD and ALD mechanisms
Choose a deposition method for a given film and topography
Compute ALD cycles and time
Diagnose film stress/peeling issues

scenes.text: A process engineer must line a 10:1 trench with 2 nm of barrier uniformly — top, walls and bottom.
Sputtering would coat the top thickly and the bottom barely; ALD coats every surface equally.

steps.title: CVD
steps.body: Gas precursors react on a heated surface. **LPCVD** (low pressure, 550–800 °C): polysilicon, nitride — good uniformity. **PECVD** (plasma, 200–400 °C): oxides/nitrides at low temperature, back-end friendly.

steps.title: PVD
steps.body: Physical vapour: **sputtering** knocks atoms off a target with Ar⁺ ions (metals, TiN, barriers); **evaporation** heats a source (used in some packaging/R&D). Line-of-sight → poor step coverage in deep features.

steps.title: ALD
steps.body: Alternating self-limiting half-reactions (e.g. TMA + H₂O for Al₂O₃; HfCl₄ + H₂O for HfO₂). Growth per cycle ~0.05–0.1 nm. Near-perfect conformality; slow.

steps.title: Epitaxy & plating
steps.body: **Epitaxy** grows single-crystal Si or SiGe on Si (strain, source/drain). **Electroplating (ECD)** fills copper interconnects.

activity.prompt: Explore deposition coverage on a trench: compare PVD and ALD films.

objects.label: Substrate with trench
objects.info: A 10:1 trench etched into a dielectric.

objects.label: PVD film (top-heavy)
objects.info: Line-of-sight sputtering: thick on top, thin on sidewalls, overhang at the opening.

objects.label: ALD film (conformal)
objects.info: Same thickness everywhere thanks to self-limiting surface reactions.

objects.label: Precursor pulse
objects.info: One precursor saturates the surface, purge, then the co-reactant completes one monolayer.

tour.text: PVD arrives line-of-sight and overhangs.
ALD saturates every surface.
Each ALD cycle: precursor pulse, purge, reactant, purge.

scenes.text: Integration sends six film requests.
Pick the right family for each.

steps.title: Decision hints
steps.body:
- Need conformality in deep features or sub-nm control → **ALD**.
- Metal or barrier on fairly open topography → **PVD**.
- Thick dielectric, moderate temperature → **PECVD/HDP-CVD**.
- Single-crystal layer → **epitaxy**.
- Fill copper → **ECD** (after PVD barrier/seed).

scenes.text: HfO₂ ALD grows about 0.1 nm per cycle; each cycle (pulse–purge–pulse–purge) takes 2 s.
How long for 3 nm?

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: 3 nm / 0.1 nm per cycle = 30 cycles × 2 s = **60 s** (plus heat-up and transfer).

steps.title: Throughput fixes
steps.body: Batch ALD furnaces, spatial ALD (wafer moves between precursor zones) and multi-station chambers keep cost down.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Growth per cycle is less than one full monolayer because precursor molecules are bulky (steric hindrance).

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — film peeling after anneal

scenes.text: A PECVD nitride film cracks and peels after a 450 °C anneal.
Work the problem.

steps.title: Film stress
steps.body: Films carry intrinsic + thermal stress (mismatched expansion). Measured by wafer bow change (Stoney equation). Too much tensile stress → cracks; compressive → buckling/delamination.

steps.title: Levers

courses.title: Ion implantation & annealing
courses.summary: Placing dopants precisely: ion source, mass analyser, acceleration, scanning; dose and energy, projected range and straggle, channelling, damage and activation anneals (spike, laser, flash).
outcomes: Describe an ion implanter's beam line
Compute implant time from beam current and dose
Estimate peak concentration from dose and straggle

story.title: A particle accelerator in a fab

scenes.text: An implanter is a small particle accelerator: it ionises BF₃, PH₃ or AsH₃, selects one ion by mass, accelerates it and fires it into the wafer.
Dose is counted by measuring the charge that arrives — like a precise ion bucket.

steps.title: Beam line
steps.body: Ion source → extraction → **analyser magnet** (selects mass/charge, e.g. ¹¹B⁺) → acceleration → beam scanning (electrostatic/mechanical) → wafer on a cooled platen with a Faraday cup for dose counting.

steps.title: Key parameters
steps.body:
- **Energy** (keV → MeV) sets depth (projected range R_p).
- **Dose** Q (ions/cm²) sets amount (10¹¹ for V_T adjust; 10¹⁵ for source/drain).
- **Tilt/twist** avoid **channelling** along crystal axes.

steps.title: Implant types
steps.body: High-current (S/D, low energy), medium-current (wells, halo), high-energy (deep wells, CMOS image sensor isolation).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Implant creates lattice damage and dopants are not yet active — an anneal is always needed.

activity.prompt: Explore the implanter beam line and tap each section.

objects.label: Ion source
objects.info: Plasma ionises dopant gas (BF₃, PH₃, AsH₃).

objects.label: Analyser magnet
objects.info: Bends ions; only the selected mass/charge passes the slit.

objects.label: Accelerator column
objects.info: Raises ions to the target energy.

objects.label: Scanner
objects.info: Sweeps the beam for uniform dose.

objects.label: Wafer + Faraday cup
objects.info: Charge collected = dose; wafer tilted ~7° to avoid channelling.

quiz.q: Implant depth is mainly set by…

lessons.title: Lab: Implant time from beam current

scenes.text: Source/drain implant: dose 1×10¹⁵ cm⁻², singly charged ions, beam current 1 mA, 300 mm wafer.
t = Q·q·A / I.

steps.title: Doubly charged ions
steps.body: For X²⁺ each ion carries 2q, so the measured charge is twice the ion count — dose counting must account for charge state.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Use the scanned area, not just the die area, and keep units consistent (cm²).

activity.prompt: Dose 5×10¹⁴ cm⁻², singly charged, beam current 2 mA, 300 mm wafer (A = 706.9 cm²). Implant time in seconds?

lessons.title: Lab: Gaussian profile and peak concentration

scenes.text: A simple model treats the as-implanted profile as Gaussian: N(x) = N_p·exp[−(x−R_p)²/(2ΔR_p²)].
Peak N_p = Q / (√(2π)·ΔR_p).

steps.title: Real profiles
steps.body: Light ions (B) skew; channelling tails appear; SIMS (secondary-ion mass spectrometry) measures real profiles.

steps.title: Annealing
steps.body: Goal: activate dopants and repair damage with minimal diffusion. Furnace (minutes) → RTA spike (~1 s) → flash/laser (ms–µs). Advanced nodes use millisecond anneals to keep junctions ultra-shallow.

activity.prompt: Q = 2×10¹³ cm⁻², ΔR_p = 50 nm. Peak concentration N_p? Enter the mantissa ×10¹⁸ cm⁻³.

steps.title: Suspects
steps.body: Dose error (Faraday cup / charge-state), energy error, tilt/twist (channelling), beam contamination (wrong species, energetic contamination), anneal variation.

steps.title: Implant monitors

courses.title: CMP & metallisation: copper damascene to backside power
courses.summary: Building the wiring skyscraper above transistors: chemical-mechanical planarisation, the Preston equation, dishing/erosion, dual-damascene copper, barriers, low-k dielectrics, RC delay, electromigration, cobalt/ruthenium and backside power delivery.
outcomes: Explain why CMP is required and compute removal rate with Preston's law
Order a dual-damascene copper module
Compute wire resistance and current density

scenes.text: Above the transistors sit 10–15+ metal layers — thin local wires at the bottom, fat global wires at the top.
Every layer must be planarised flat, or the next litho step goes out of focus.

steps.title: Back end of line (BEOL)
steps.body: Contacts/local interconnect (often tungsten/cobalt) → M1…Mn copper in low-k dielectric → top thick metals for power and clocks → passivation and bond pads.

steps.title: Damascene
steps.body: Etch trenches/vias into dielectric, line with barrier (TaN/Ta), deposit Cu seed, electroplate copper, then **CMP** away the excess. 'Dual' = via + trench filled in one step.

steps.title: Why not etch copper
steps.body: Copper does not form volatile etch products easily, so it is inlaid (damascene) instead of etched like aluminium was.

steps.title: Backside power
steps.body: Leading-edge processes are moving power wires to the wafer back (backside power delivery), freeing front-side tracks for signals and cutting IR drop.

activity.prompt: Explode the chip package and its metal stack to see wiring layers above the transistors.

tour.text: The die sits on a substrate inside the package.
Explode: transistors at the bottom, metal layers above.

options: power wiring to the wafer back

scenes.text: CMP presses the wafer face-down on a rotating pad with slurry (abrasive + chemistry).
Preston: RR = K_p · P · V.

steps.title: Defects
steps.body:
- **Dishing**: wide copper lines get over-polished (concave).
- **Erosion**: dense arrays thin the dielectric.
- Scratches, residues, corrosion. Fixes: dummy fill patterns, selective slurries, multi-step polish, end-point (motor current/optical).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Preston's law is empirical — K_p depends on slurry, pad, film and temperature, so it must be calibrated.

steps.title: Low-k care
steps.body: Porous low-k is mechanically weak and damaged by plasma; integration must protect it.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — wire resistance and electromigration

scenes.text: Timing shows a 1 mm local route is too slow.
Compute its resistance: ρ = 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m (bulk Cu; real narrow wires are worse), W = 50 nm, T = 100 nm.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: A = 50e-9 × 100e-9 = 5×10⁻¹⁵ m². R = ρL/A = 1.7e-8 × 1e-3 / 5e-15 = **3,400 Ω** — and narrow lines have higher effective ρ due to surface/grain scattering and barrier area.

steps.title: Electromigration
steps.body: High current density pushes metal atoms, forming voids and hillocks. Design rules cap J (order of MA/cm² for Cu at operating temperature). J = I/A.

steps.title: Fixes
steps.body: Route long nets on upper, thicker metals; insert repeaters; use wider wires; new metals (Co, Ru) at the tightest pitches where barrier-less fill wins.

courses.title: Transistor architectures: planar → FinFET → GAA → CFET
courses.summary: Why the transistor went 3D: short-channel effects, electrostatic control, FinFET geometry and effective width, nanosheet gate-all-around, forksheet and complementary FET concepts, and what 'node names' really mean.
outcomes: Explain short-channel effects and why gate control matters
Compute FinFET and nanosheet effective width
Compare planar, FinFET and GAA trade-offs
Read a transistor roadmap critically

scenes.text: At around the 22–16 nm generation, planar transistors leaked too much: the drain started controlling the channel.
The fix: wrap the gate around a thin silicon fin.

steps.title: Short-channel effects
steps.body:
- **DIBL**: drain voltage lowers the source barrier.
- **V_T roll-off**: V_T falls with shorter L.
- **Sub-threshold swing** degrades (ideal limit ≈ 60 mV/decade at 300 K).
All arise because the gate loses electrostatic control vs the drain.

steps.title: FinFET
steps.body: A tall thin fin (width ~5–8 nm at advanced nodes) with gate on three sides. Width is quantised: you add fins, not continuous W.

steps.title: GAA nanosheet
steps.body: Stacked horizontal silicon sheets with the gate on all four sides — best control, and sheet width can vary per device. Made from a Si/SiGe superlattice where SiGe is selectively removed (channel release), then the gate fills the gaps.

steps.title: Next
steps.body: Forksheet (dielectric wall between n and p sheets) and **CFET** (nMOS stacked on pMOS) are research/roadmap directions to shrink cell area further.

activity.prompt: Explode a FinFET: fin, gate wrapping three sides, source/drain and spacers.

tour.text: The silicon fin is the channel.
The gate wraps the top and both sides.
Explode: gate metal, high-k, fin, epi source/drain.
In GAA the gate also covers the bottom of each sheet.

scenes.text: A FinFET's electrical width per fin ≈ 2·H_fin + W_fin.
H_fin = 50 nm, W_fin = 7 nm, 3 fins.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: Per fin: 2 × 50 + 7 = 107 nm. Three fins: **321 nm**.

steps.title: Footprint advantage
steps.body: Fin pitch ~30 nm: three fins occupy ~90 nm of layout width yet give 321 nm of electrical width — that is the 3D density win.

steps.title: Quantisation
steps.body: You cannot have 2.5 fins — designers pick 1, 2, 3… fins, which constrains analog and SRAM sizing.

activity.prompt: H_fin = 45 nm, W_fin = 6 nm, 4 fins. Total effective width in nm?

scenes.text: Nanosheet width per sheet ≈ 2·(W_sheet + T_sheet).
3 sheets, W = 30 nm, T = 5 nm.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: Per sheet: 2 × (30 + 5) = 70 nm. Three sheets: **210 nm**.

steps.title: Design benefit
steps.body: Sheet width can be drawn per device (e.g. 15–45 nm), giving finer drive-strength choices than fin counts.

steps.title: Process challenges
steps.body: Inner spacers between sheets, selective SiGe removal, gate metal filling tiny gaps, and channel stress engineering.

activity.prompt: 4 sheets, W = 25 nm, T = 6 nm. Total effective width in nm?

options: better gate control and variable width

steps.title: Node names
steps.body: Generations like '7 nm', '3 nm', '2 nm' are labels; compare density (transistors/mm²), performance and power, not the name.

steps.title: Why gate-last
steps.body: High-k/metal gates cannot survive the high-temperature S/D anneals, so a sacrificial poly gate is used first and replaced later.

steps.body: Control charts flag out-of-control signals: a point beyond 3σ, runs of points on one side of the mean, trends. Out-of-control ≠ out-of-spec, but it means something changed.

courses.title: How the chip industry is organised: IDM, foundry, fabless, OSAT
courses.summary: Who does what in semiconductors: integrated device manufacturers, pure-play foundries, fabless designers, OSAT/ATMP, EDA and IP vendors, equipment and materials suppliers — explained neutrally with well-known examples.
outcomes: Classify companies by business model

scenes.text: The SoC in a phone may be designed by one company, using CPU IP licensed from another, EDA tools from a third, made by a foundry, and packaged by an OSAT.
Each specialises because each step is enormously complex.

steps.title: Business models
steps.body:
- **IDM** (integrated device manufacturer): designs and makes its own chips (examples: Intel, Samsung, Texas Instruments, Infineon, Micron).
- **Foundry**: manufactures chips designed by others (examples: TSMC, GlobalFoundries, UMC, SMIC; Samsung and Intel also offer foundry services).
- **Fabless**: designs only (examples: NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, MediaTek, Broadcom).
- **OSAT/ATMP**: outsourced assembly and test (examples: ASE, Amkor, JCET).

steps.title: Enablers
steps.body:
- **EDA** software (Synopsys, Cadence, Siemens EDA).
- **IP** cores (Arm CPU IP, interface IP).
- **Equipment** (ASML, Applied Materials, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron, KLA).
- **Materials** (wafers, gases, chemicals, photoresists, substrates).

steps.title: Why fabless works
steps.body: A leading-edge fab costs tens of billions of dollars. Pooling many customers' demand in one foundry spreads that cost; designers avoid fab risk.

steps.title: Neutral view
steps.body: Company lists are examples, not rankings or endorsements; market positions change over time.

courses.title: The global semiconductor supply chain & resilience
courses.summary: Following a chip around the world: design, IP, equipment, materials, wafer fab, ATMP and distribution; geographic concentration, lead times, the bullwhip effect, shortages, and how companies and countries build resilience.

scenes.text: A single chip may cross many borders before it reaches a phone factory.
Design in one country, equipment from others, fab in another, packaging somewhere else.

steps.title: Geography (broad picture)
steps.body:
- Chip design and EDA: strong presence in the United States, with large design centres in India, Europe, Israel, Taiwan, China and elsewhere.
- Equipment: concentrated in the US, the Netherlands and Japan.
- Materials and wafers: Japan is a major supplier; others in Korea, Taiwan, Europe, US.
- Leading-edge logic fabs: concentrated in East Asia (especially Taiwan and South Korea), with new fabs being built in the US, Japan and Europe.
- Assembly & test: Taiwan, China, Southeast Asia (e.g. Malaysia, Vietnam), and growing in India.

steps.title: Indian design talent
steps.body: India hosts a large share of the world's chip-design engineers, working in design centres of many global companies.

lessons.title: Lab: Mock interview — process / yield engineer

scenes.text: You're interviewing for a process engineer role in an etch/deposition module.
Answer each question as if speaking to the hiring manager.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Context → data you'd look at → hypotheses → actions → verification → prevention.

steps.title: Know your numbers
steps.body: Rayleigh R = k₁λ/NA; Deal–Grove; Cpk; Poisson yield; ISO classes; implant dose time.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Always mention safety (chemicals, gases, LOTO) and containment first in incident questions.

rounds.q: Inline inspection shows particle adders jumped after your etch chamber. What do you do?
rounds.model: First I'd contain: inhibit the suspect chamber and hold affected lots. Then commonality analysis to confirm which chamber and time window, SEM/EDX review to classify the defects, and a check of PM history and RF hours. If walls are flaking, wet clean and season the chamber, qualify with particle monitors, then disposition lots with yield engineering. Finally I'd add an MES interlock so PM intervals can't be exceeded.
followups: How would you decide whether to scrap or release held lots?

rounds.q: Explain Cpk to a non-engineer and say what value you'd want.
rounds.model: Cpk tells us how comfortably a process fits inside its spec limits. It takes the distance from the average to the nearest limit and divides by three standard deviations. A Cpk of 1.0 means the nearest limit is just three sigma away; many fabs want at least 1.33. You improve it by centring the process and reducing variation.
followups: Cpk vs Ppk?

rounds.q: Why did the industry adopt EUV if DUV multi-patterning works?
rounds.model: DUV immersion at 193 nm can print tight pitches only with multiple exposures, adding masks, steps, overlay error and cycle time. EUV at 13.5 nm prints critical layers in a single exposure, simplifying the flow and improving overlay, though it brings challenges such as stochastic defects and source power. The decision is a cost, yield and capacity trade-off per layer.
followups: What does High-NA change?

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you solved a hard problem with data.
rounds.model: Use STAR: describe the situation, your task, the specific actions you took with data (e.g. analysing logs, designing an experiment), and a measurable result. Close with what you learned.
followups: What would you do differently?

rounds.q: A furnace shows oxide 4% thin only in some slots. How do you approach it?
rounds.model: I'd map thickness by slot with monitor wafers to see the spatial pattern. Slot-specific thinning points to a temperature zone, so I'd compare profile and spike thermocouples and check zone power. I'd also rule out gas flow. After fixing (e.g. a drifting thermocouple), I'd re-profile and verify uniformity on all slots before releasing.
followups: What if it were wafer-to-wafer random instead?

tips: Structure: context → approach → numbers → trade-offs → how you'd verify.

lessons.title: Lab: Mock interview — RTL / design verification engineer

scenes.text: Interview for an RTL/DV role at a design centre.
Mix of technical and coding-concept questions.

steps.title: Whiteboard
steps.body: Draw timing diagrams; talk through edge-by-edge behaviour.

steps.title: Common topics
steps.body: Blocking vs non-blocking, latches, CDC (clock-domain crossing), FSMs, setup/hold, FIFOs, coverage, UVM basics.

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: Read the task once fully. Note what 'done' looks like, then work step by step. If you get stuck, use the hint — then try again without it.

rounds.q: What's the difference between blocking and non-blocking assignments, and where do you use each?
rounds.model: Blocking (=) executes in order inside a procedural block, so later statements see updated values — use it in combinational always @(*) blocks. Non-blocking (<=) samples all right-hand sides first and updates together at the end of the time step, modelling flip-flops — use it in clocked blocks. Mixing them causes simulation races and synthesis mismatches.
followups: Show a swap example.

rounds.q: How can a latch be inferred and why is it bad?
rounds.model: A latch is inferred when a combinational block doesn't assign an output in every path, so the tool must hold the old value. Latches complicate timing analysis, can glitch and are usually unintended. Fix it by assigning defaults at the top or covering every branch, including a default case.
followups: When are latches intentional?

rounds.q: Compute setup slack: T=1 ns, clk-to-Q 50 ps, logic 800 ps, setup 40 ps, capture clock +20 ps late.
rounds.model: Setup slack = period + skew − (clk-to-Q + logic + setup) = 1000 + 20 − 890 = +130 ps, so it meets timing.
followups: Now compute hold if min logic is 10 ps and hold is 30 ps.

rounds.q: How do you safely pass a single-bit signal between two unrelated clock domains?
rounds.model: For a single-bit level signal, use a two- (or three-) flop synchroniser in the destination domain to reduce metastability risk. Pulses need stretching or a handshake. Multi-bit values need Gray-coded pointers in an asynchronous FIFO or a handshake protocol, never independent bit synchronisers.
followups: How would you verify CDC?

rounds.q: Your regression fails on 3% of seeds. Walk me through triage.
rounds.model: I'd reproduce with the failing seed and dump waves, find the first scoreboard mismatch, decide whether the reference model or RTL is wrong, and diff recent changes. I'd write a minimal directed test, file the bug with seed and waveform, and after the fix add the test and a covergroup so it can't regress.
followups: How do you prioritise multiple failing signatures?

rounds.q: Why do you want to work in chip design?
rounds.model: Give a specific, honest reason (e.g. a project you built), connect it to the role, and show you're eager to learn the team's flow.

tips: Structure: context → approach → numbers → trade-offs → how you'd verify.

options: async FIFO with Gray pointers or handshake

lessons.title: Lab: Mock interview — packaging / test engineer

scenes.text: Interview for a packaging and test engineering role.
Expect yield, reliability and troubleshooting questions.

steps.title: Talk numbers
steps.body: Die-per-wafer, Poisson yield, Arrhenius AF, FIT — be ready to compute on the spot.

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: Read the task once fully. Note what 'done' looks like, then work step by step. If you get stuck, use the hint — then try again without it.

steps.title: Check your work
steps.body: When you finish, verify the result the way a professional would: re-run the check, compare with the expected output, and write one line about what you learned.

rounds.q: Compare wire-bond and flip-chip packaging.
rounds.model: Wire bonding connects perimeter pads with thin wires — cheap and mature but limited I/O and higher inductance. Flip-chip places bumps across the die face, giving many more I/O and power connections, shorter paths and better thermal routes through the die back, but needs bumping, substrates and underfill, so it costs more.
followups: When would you still choose wire bond?

rounds.q: Compute the Arrhenius acceleration factor for Ea 0.7 eV from 55 °C use to 125 °C stress.
rounds.model: Convert to kelvin: 328.15 and 398.15 K. AF = exp[(0.7/8.617e-5)(1/328.15 − 1/398.15)] ≈ exp(4.35) ≈ 78. So 1,000 hours of HTOL represents roughly 78,000 field hours for that mechanism.
followups: Why can't one AF cover all mechanisms?

rounds.q: Continuity failures jumped on one prober. What do you do?
rounds.model: I'd re-test a failing wafer on another qualified prober and card to separate wafer vs test-cell issues. If it passes elsewhere, I'd inspect the original card's tips and planarity and check overdrive. After repair, I'd verify on a card analyser and re-test held wafers, then add a post-maintenance planarity check.
followups: How do you avoid pad damage?

rounds.q: Why do chiplets improve yield economics?
rounds.model: Yield falls exponentially with die area, so smaller chiplets yield much better; with known-good-die testing only good chiplets are assembled. You can also put I/O on a cheaper node. The trade-offs are die-to-die interface overhead, packaging cost and assembly yield.
followups: What is UCIe?

rounds.q: Describe a time you disagreed with a colleague. How did you handle it?
rounds.model: Use STAR: explain the disagreement, how you listened and used data to find common ground, and the result. Show respect and focus on the problem, not the person.

tips: Structure: context → approach → numbers → trade-offs → how you'd verify.

tech-semi-physics.title: Semiconductor physics for makers
tech-semi-physics.description: From band gaps and doping to PN junctions, MOSFETs and real bench testing — the physics behind every chip, with number labs you can check. Goes deeper than circuit courses: what happens inside the silicon.

courses.title: Energy bands & intrinsic silicon
courses.summary: Why silicon is a semiconductor: atoms, covalent bonds, energy bands, band gap, electrons and holes, and the intrinsic carrier concentration — explained for makers who want to understand what is inside every chip.
outcomes: Explain conductors, insulators and semiconductors using band gaps
Describe electrons and holes as charge carriers
Compute photon cut-off wavelength from band gap

lessons.title: Atoms to bands: why silicon is special

scenes.text: Asha's solar lamp charges in sunlight but not under a red LED torch at night.
Her teacher says the answer is the band gap of silicon — the energy 'toll' an electron must pay to conduct.

steps.title: Covalent crystal
steps.body: Silicon has 4 valence electrons. In a crystal each atom shares one electron with each of 4 neighbours (diamond-cubic lattice, lattice constant ≈ 0.543 nm). At absolute zero every electron is locked in a bond — pure silicon is an insulator.

steps.title: Bands, not levels
steps.body:
When ~5×10²² atoms/cm³ sit close together, their discrete energy levels spread into **bands**.

- **Valence band**: the bonding electrons.
- **Conduction band**: electrons free to move.
- **Band gap Eg**: forbidden energies between them. Si ≈ 1.12 eV, Ge ≈ 0.66 eV, GaAs ≈ 1.42 eV, SiO₂ ≈ 9 eV at room temperature.

steps.title: Holes are real carriers
steps.body: When an electron jumps to the conduction band it leaves a vacancy in a bond — a **hole**. Neighbouring bond electrons hop into it, so the hole moves like a positive charge. Current = electron flow + hole flow.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: A hole is not a positron and not 'nothing'; it is the collective motion of many valence electrons, modelled as one +q particle with its own effective mass and mobility.

activity.prompt: Rotate the silicon crystal model. Each sphere is an atom with four bonds; tap to see what happens when a bond breaks.

objects.label: Si atom
objects.info: Silicon atom with 4 valence electrons shared with neighbours.

objects.label: Neighbour Si
objects.info: Each Si has four nearest neighbours in a tetrahedron.

objects.label: Neighbour Si
objects.info: Bond angle ≈ 109.5° — the tetrahedral angle.

objects.label: Neighbour Si
objects.info: Bond = a shared pair of electrons.

objects.label: Free electron
objects.info: Thermal energy ≥ Eg broke a bond: this electron is now in the conduction band.

objects.label: Hole
objects.info: The broken bond left behind behaves like a +q carrier.

lessons.title: Lab: Photon cut-off wavelength from the band gap

scenes.text: Ravi is choosing a photodiode for a 940 nm IR remote receiver.
He needs λ = hc/Eg to see if silicon can absorb it.

steps.title: The rule
steps.body: A photon can create an electron–hole pair only if E_photon ≥ Eg. With E in eV and λ in nm: **λ_max ≈ 1240 / Eg**.

steps.title: Worked: silicon
steps.body: λ_max = 1240 / 1.12 ≈ 1107 nm. 940 nm IR (1.32 eV) is absorbed → silicon photodiodes work for TV remotes. 1550 nm telecom light (0.80 eV) is NOT absorbed by Si → telecom uses InGaAs or Ge.

steps.title: Worked: LEDs
steps.body: Direct-gap materials emit near their gap: GaAs (1.42 eV) emits ≈ 870 nm IR; GaN-based (≈2.7 eV with indium) emits blue ≈ 450 nm.

steps.title: Direct vs indirect
steps.body: Silicon is an **indirect** gap material: it absorbs light but emits it very poorly, which is why LEDs and lasers use III-V compounds.

activity.prompt: GaAs has Eg = 1.42 eV. What is its cut-off wavelength λ_max in nm (use λ = 1240/Eg)?

quiz.q: Why is silicon a poor LED material?

lessons.title: Lab: Intrinsic carriers and thermal voltage

scenes.text: A dash-cam sensor gets noisy in a 70 °C parked car.
Intrinsic carrier density rises steeply with temperature — that is the 'dark current'.

steps.title: Intrinsic concentration
steps.body: In pure Si, n = p = nᵢ. At 300 K nᵢ ≈ 1×10¹⁰ cm⁻³ (textbooks quote 1.0–1.5×10¹⁰). It follows nᵢ ∝ T^{3/2}·exp(−Eg/2kT): roughly doubling every ~11 °C near room temperature.

steps.title: Mass-action law
steps.body: In equilibrium, **n·p = nᵢ²** always — doped or not. This single equation lets you find minority carriers.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Do not use 26 mV at every temperature. At 125 °C (398 K) V_T ≈ 34.3 mV — automotive designs must account for this.

activity.prompt: Compute V_T = kT/q at 398 K (125 °C) in millivolts. k = 1.381×10⁻²³ J/K, q = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C.

quiz.why: Intrinsic means equal electrons and holes.
Holds in equilibrium for doped and undoped material.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — classify materials by band gap

scenes.text: A start-up asks you which materials suit a solar cell, a blue LED, a gate insulator and a power transistor.
Sort them by band-gap class to brief the team.

steps.title: Gap classes
steps.body:
- **Narrow (< 1 eV)**: Ge, InSb — IR detectors.
- **Moderate (1–2 eV)**: Si, GaAs — logic, solar, IR LEDs.
- **Wide (> 2.5 eV)**: SiC (~3.3 eV for 4H), GaN (3.4 eV) — power electronics, blue/UV LEDs.
- **Insulators (> 5 eV)**: SiO₂, Si₃N₄, HfO₂ (~5.7 eV).

steps.title: Why wide-gap for power
steps.body: Wide-gap materials withstand much higher electric fields before breakdown and work hotter, so EV inverters and fast chargers increasingly use SiC and GaN.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Memorise a short table of Eg values — GATE and interviews ask them often.

lessons.title: Donors, acceptors and the Fermi level

scenes.text: Neha's first fab job: a wafer box says 'P-type, Boron, 10 Ω·cm, <100>'.
She wants to know what each part means.

steps.title: n-type
steps.body: Group-V atoms (P, As, Sb) have 5 valence electrons; 4 bond and the 5th is loosely bound (~0.045 eV for P) and ionises at room temperature → **donor**. Electrons become majority carriers.

steps.title: p-type
steps.body: Group-III atoms (B, also Al, Ga, In) have 3 electrons; the missing bond is a hole → **acceptor**. Holes become majority carriers. Boron is the standard p-type dopant in Si.

steps.title: Tiny amounts
steps.body: A 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ dopant level is ~1 dopant per 5 million Si atoms — yet it raises conductivity by about a million times.

steps.title: Fermi level
steps.body: The Fermi level E_F sits mid-gap in intrinsic Si, moves towards the conduction band in n-type and towards the valence band in p-type: E_F − Eᵢ = kT·ln(n/nᵢ).

activity.prompt: Explore a doped lattice. Tap the donor and the acceptor and read what each contributes.

objects.info: 5 valence electrons: the extra one is freed at room temperature → n-type.

objects.label: Donated electron
objects.info: Majority carrier in n-type silicon.

objects.label: Boron (acceptor)
objects.info: 3 valence electrons: one bond incomplete → a hole, p-type.

objects.label: Hole
objects.info: Majority carrier in p-type silicon.

lessons.title: Lab: Minority carriers with the mass-action law

scenes.text: A diode's reverse leakage depends on minority carriers.
You need p in an n-type region doped at 10¹⁶ cm⁻³.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ ≫ nᵢ, so n ≈ N_D = 10¹⁶. p = nᵢ²/n = (10¹⁰)² / 10¹⁶ = **10⁴ cm⁻³**.

steps.title: Worked 2
steps.body: p-type N_A = 5×10¹⁷ cm⁻³: n = 10²⁰ / 5×10¹⁷ = 200 cm⁻³.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Do not add donor and intrinsic densities. If N_D ≫ nᵢ, n ≈ N_D. Only near intrinsic levels (N_D ~ nᵢ) solve the quadratic n = N_D/2 + √((N_D/2)² + nᵢ²).

steps.title: Conductivity
steps.body: σ = q(n·μn + p·μp). For n-type, σ ≈ q·N_D·μn. ρ = 1/σ. Mobility in lightly doped Si: μn ≈ 1350, μp ≈ 480 cm²/V·s (falls at higher doping).

steps.title: Drift and diffusion
steps.body: Drift current follows the electric field; diffusion current follows the concentration gradient. Einstein relation: D/μ = kT/q, so Dn ≈ 1350 × 0.0259 ≈ 35 cm²/s.

steps.title: Sanity check
steps.body: Real wafers: 1–20 Ω·cm for CMOS substrates means doping around 10¹⁴–10¹⁵ cm⁻³ — lightly doped.

scenes.text: A box of 25 wafers arrives: 'N-type, Phos, 1–5 Ω·cm, <100>, 300 mm, 775 µm'.

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body:
- **N-type, Phos**: dopant and type.
- **1–5 Ω·cm**: resistivity range (→ doping ≈ 1–5×10¹⁵ cm⁻³).
- **<100>**: crystal orientation of the surface (CMOS standard).
- **300 mm / 775 µm**: diameter and thickness (SEMI standard for 300 mm).

steps.title: Why orientation
steps.body: <100> gives lower interface-trap density at the Si/SiO₂ interface, so MOSFETs perform better; <111> was used for older bipolar processes.

steps.title: Type check
steps.body: A hot-probe or the four-point probe plus a type tester confirms n vs p before use.

courses.title: The PN junction & diodes
courses.summary: Depletion region, built-in potential, forward and reverse bias, the Shockley diode equation, breakdown, LEDs and solar cells — with real maker calculations.
outcomes: Explain how a depletion region and built-in potential form
Compute built-in voltage from doping
Use the diode equation and the 60 mV/decade rule
Size an LED resistor and read a solar cell I–V curve

scenes.text: Imagine pressing p-type and n-type silicon together (in reality the junction is made by implant or diffusion).
Electrons and holes diffuse across and recombine, leaving fixed ions behind — a tiny built-in battery forms.

steps.title: Depletion region
steps.body: Near the junction, mobile carriers recombine, leaving ionised donors (+) on the n side and acceptors (−) on the p side. This **space-charge region** has an electric field that opposes further diffusion.

steps.title: Built-in potential
steps.body: V_bi = V_T · ln(N_A·N_D / nᵢ²). Typical Si junctions: 0.6–0.9 V. You cannot measure V_bi with a voltmeter — contact potentials cancel it.

steps.title: Bias
steps.body:
- **Forward** (p to +): barrier lowers, current rises exponentially.
- **Reverse**: barrier rises, depletion widens, only a tiny saturation current flows — until breakdown (Zener or avalanche).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: The depletion region extends further into the **lightly** doped side (charge balance N_A·x_p = N_D·x_n).

activity.prompt: Explore a PN junction in 3D: p region, n region and the depletion layer between them.

objects.label: p-type region
objects.info: Acceptor-doped; holes are majority carriers.

objects.label: Depletion region
objects.info: No mobile carriers; fixed ions create the built-in field.

objects.label: n-type region
objects.info: Donor-doped; electrons are majority carriers.

objects.label: Built-in field
objects.info: Points from n (+ions) to p (−ions).

tour.text: The p side holds acceptor ions and mobile holes.
The depletion layer has fixed charge only.
The built-in field opposes diffusion.

steps.title: Worked 2
steps.body: N_A = N_D = 10¹⁵: ratio 10¹⁰ → ln = 23.03 → V_bi ≈ 0.595 V. Heavier doping → larger V_bi.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.body: Each ×10 in the doping product adds V_T·ln10 ≈ 59.5 mV.

scenes.text: Kabir wants to drive a red LED (Vf ≈ 2.0 V at 15 mA) from a 5 V Arduino pin.

steps.title: Shockley equation
steps.body: I = I_s·(e^{V/(n·V_T)} − 1). For n = 1, current rises **10× per ≈ 59.5 mV** (V_T·ln10). That steepness is why you control LED current with a resistor or a constant-current driver, not a voltage.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: R = (V_supply − V_f)/I = (5 − 2.0)/0.015 = **200 Ω** → nearest E12 value 220 Ω gives ≈ 13.6 mA.

steps.title: Power
steps.body: P_R = I²R = 0.015² × 200 = 45 mW → a 1/4 W resistor is fine.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Blue/white LEDs have V_f ≈ 2.8–3.3 V; using the red-LED value overdrives nothing but gives wrong brightness — always read the datasheet.

courses.title: MOSFET operation — the transistor in every chip
courses.summary: MOS capacitor, threshold voltage, inversion, the square-law model, regions of operation, scaling, leakage and dynamic power — the physics behind billions of switches per chip.
outcomes: Describe accumulation, depletion and inversion in a MOS capacitor
Compute gate-oxide capacitance
Compute drain current with the square-law model
Compute CMOS dynamic power and explain why scaling slowed

scenes.text: Metal (gate) – Oxide (insulator) – Semiconductor (channel). Today the 'metal' is a metal gate on a high-k oxide.
A voltage on the gate, not a current, controls the switch.

steps.title: MOS capacitor
steps.body:
For a p-type substrate:
- V_G < 0: holes pile up → **accumulation**.
- Small V_G > 0: holes pushed away → **depletion**.
- V_G > V_T: electrons gather at the surface → **inversion**: an n-channel forms.

steps.title: nMOS and pMOS
steps.body: nMOS: n⁺ source/drain in p-substrate, conducts when V_GS > V_T. pMOS: p⁺ in n-well, conducts when V_GS < −|V_T|. CMOS uses both so one is always off in steady state.

steps.title: Threshold
steps.body: V_T depends on doping, oxide thickness, gate work function and fixed charges. Modern logic V_T ≈ 0.2–0.4 V.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Gate current is (ideally) zero — the gate is a capacitor. Power is spent charging and discharging it, not holding it.

activity.prompt: Explode the CMOS inverter: one nMOS and one pMOS sharing a gate input.

tour.text: The pMOS connects the output to VDD when the input is low.
The nMOS connects the output to ground when the input is high.
Explode the layers: gate, oxide, channel, wells.

quiz.q: Inversion in a p-substrate nMOS creates…

scenes.text: Old 1 µm processes used ~20 nm oxide; advanced nodes reach an equivalent oxide thickness under 1 nm using high-k HfO₂.
Compute Cox = εox/tox.

steps.title: Why high-k
steps.body: Below ~1.2 nm SiO₂, electrons tunnel through the gate → huge leakage. HfO₂ (k ≈ 20–25) gives the same capacitance with a physically thicker layer. EOT = t_highk × 3.9/k.

steps.title: EOT
steps.body: 3 nm of HfO₂ with k = 20: EOT = 3 × 3.9/20 = 0.585 nm.

activity.prompt: Compute Cox for tox = 5 nm SiO₂ (εox = 3.45×10⁻¹¹ F/m). Give the answer in fF/µm².

quiz.q: Why HfO₂ instead of very thin SiO₂?

scenes.text: Long-channel model: in saturation I_D = ½·μnCox·(W/L)·(V_GS − V_T)².
μnCox = 200 µA/V², W/L = 10, V_T = 0.5 V.

steps.title: Regions
steps.body:
- **Cut-off**: V_GS < V_T, I_D ≈ 0 (sub-threshold leakage).
- **Linear/triode**: V_DS < V_GS − V_T, I_D = μnCox(W/L)[(V_GS−V_T)V_DS − V_DS²/2].
- **Saturation**: V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T, square law.

steps.title: Short channels
steps.body: In modern short-channel devices velocity saturation makes I_D closer to linear in overdrive; the square law is a teaching model, not a sign-off model (foundries give BSIM models).

Dynamic power P = α·C·V²·f; leakage adds static power.

steps.title: DVFS
steps.body: Lowering V is the strongest lever (V²). Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling drops both under light load.

steps.title: End of Dennard scaling
steps.body: Until ~2005 shrinking transistors kept power density constant. Because V_T and V_DD could not keep shrinking (leakage), power density rose — hence multicore, power gating and dark silicon.

courses.summary: Practical semiconductor skills on the workbench: identify and test diodes and MOSFETs with a multimeter, choose logic-level MOSFETs, compute heat, and protect circuits with flyback diodes.

scenes.text: Isha bought a cheap power MOSFET to switch a 12 V fan from an ESP32 (3.3 V).

steps.title: Key MOSFET specs
steps.body:
- **V_DS(max)**: blocking voltage — pick ≥ 1.5–2× the supply.
- **I_D**: continuous current (at a specified case temperature).
- **R_DS(on) @ V_GS**: on-resistance *at a stated gate voltage* — the spec that matters.
- **V_GS(th)**: where it *starts* to conduct, not where it is fully on.
- **Q_g**: gate charge, sets switching speed.

steps.title: Classic trap
steps.body: A V_GS(th) of 2–4 V does NOT mean 3.3 V is enough. Look for R_DS(on) specified at V_GS = 2.5 V or 3.3 V ('logic-level').

steps.title: Diode specs
steps.body: V_F at a current, I_F(avg), V_RRM (reverse voltage), t_rr (recovery time). Schottky diodes: low V_F (~0.3–0.5 V), fast, but higher leakage.

steps.title: Diode test mode
steps.body: Forward: a silicon diode reads ≈ 0.5–0.7 V, Schottky ≈ 0.2–0.4 V, LED often glows faintly at 1.6–3 V. Reverse: 'OL'. Both directions ~0 V → shorted; both OL → open.

steps.title: MOSFET (n-channel)
steps.body: Body diode: red on Source, black on Drain → ≈ 0.5 V. Touch gate with red (charges it) → D–S then conducts; short G–S to discharge → off again. D–S near 0 Ω in both directions with gate discharged → shorted.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Power off and discharge capacitors before probing. Handle MOSFETs with ESD care — gates are sensitive.

lessons.title: Lab: Heat in a MOSFET switch

scenes.text: A MOSFET switches 3 A of LEDs. R_DS(on) = 20 mΩ at your gate drive.
Will it need a heatsink?

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: P = I²·R = 3² × 0.020 = **0.18 W**. In a small package with R_θJA = 62 °C/W: ΔT = 0.18 × 62 ≈ 11 °C. Fine without heatsink.

steps.title: Bad choice
steps.body: Same load with a non-logic MOSFET only half on, R ≈ 0.5 Ω: P = 9 × 0.5 = 4.5 W → ΔT ≈ 279 °C → it will fail.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: T_J = T_A + P·R_θJA. Keep T_J well below the datasheet max (often 150–175 °C).

scenes.text: A hobbyist's ESP32 resets every time a 12 V relay turns off.

steps.title: Flyback diode
steps.body: Place a diode across the coil (cathode to +12 V). When the switch opens, coil current circulates through the diode instead of spiking the MOSFET drain.

steps.title: Gate resistor & pulldown
steps.body: 100 Ω series gate resistor limits ringing; 10–100 kΩ gate-to-source pulldown keeps the MOSFET off while the MCU boots.

steps.title: Separate grounds wisely
steps.body: Return high current to the supply via a short path; tie MCU ground at one point.

choices.feedback: Yes — the floating gate was turning the MOSFET on.

choices.label: Remove the gate resistor
choices.feedback: That increases ringing; boot issue remains.

c.text: The problem persists. Re-examine the circuit.

choices.label: Go back and add the flyback diode

lessons.title: SOC roles and the SIEM pipeline

scenes.text: At 02:00 a SIEM alert fires: 'Multiple failed logons followed by success'. Tier-1 analyst Isha has ten minutes to decide if it is real.
She follows the pipeline: log source -> collection -> normalisation -> correlation -> alert -> triage -> escalate or close.

steps.title: SOC
steps.body: A Security Operations Centre monitors, detects, investigates and coordinates response. Typical tiers: **Tier 1** triage, **Tier 2** investigation, **Tier 3 / hunt / detection engineering**, plus an incident manager and threat-intel function. Metrics: **MTTD** (time to detect) and **MTTR** (time to respond/resolve).

steps.title: SIEM pipeline
steps.body: Log sources (firewalls, DNS, endpoints, identity, cloud, email) are **collected** by agents/syslog/API, **parsed and normalised** to a common schema, **enriched** (asset, user, geo, threat intel), **correlated** by rules, and stored for search. Time sync (NTP) and consistent time zones (UTC) make timelines reliable.

steps.title: Alert outcomes
steps.body: **True positive** (real malicious activity), **false positive** (benign but flagged), **benign true positive** (real but expected, e.g. a pen test), **false negative** (missed). Tuning reduces false positives without creating false negatives.

steps.title: Log anatomy
steps.body: A syslog-style line: **timestamp, host, process[pid], message**. In sshd lines, the message holds the outcome (`Failed password`, `Accepted publickey`), the user, the source IP and port.

steps.title: Toolbox
steps.body: `grep PATTERN file` filters lines; `grep -c` counts; `grep -v` excludes; `awk '{print $N}'` prints field N; `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` ranks values by count; `head`, `tail`, `less` navigate. `cut -d' ' -f1` also extracts fields.

steps.title: Top attackers
steps.body: grep 'Failed password' auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn -> counts failures per source IP.

steps.title: Headers
steps.body: Read **bottom-up** the `Received:` chain; check `From`, `Reply-To`, `Return-Path`, `Authentication-Results` (spf/dkim/dmarc = pass/fail). **SPF** authorises sending IPs for a domain, **DKIM** signs the message, **DMARC** ties them to the visible From domain and states policy (none/quarantine/reject).

lessons.title: Types of intel and the Pyramid of Pain

scenes.text: A vendor feed adds 50,000 file hashes a day. Isha wonders why attackers aren't stopped by blocking them all.
Your turn: read the key ideas, then apply them hands-on in the activity that follows.

steps.title: Types
steps.body: **Strategic** (trends and risk for leaders), **operational** (campaigns, actor behaviour), **tactical** (specific IOCs and TTPs for detection), **technical** (raw indicators).

steps.title: Pyramid of Pain
steps.body: From trivial to painful for the attacker: **hash values**, IP addresses, domain names, network/host artifacts, tools, and **TTPs** (tactics, techniques, procedures). Detecting behaviours at the top forces attackers to change how they work; blocking a hash costs them a recompile.

steps.title: ATT&CK
steps.body: MITRE ATT&CK is a knowledge base of adversary tactics (the why) and techniques (the how), e.g. Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Credential Access, Exfiltration. Technique examples: T1566 Phishing, T1110 Brute Force, T1078 Valid Accounts, T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Treating a feed as truth: indicators age quickly and may be shared infrastructure; always check confidence, age and context.

steps.body: **Firewall/NetFlow** (who talked to whom, ports, bytes), **DNS logs** (every name looked up), **proxy logs** (URLs, user agents), **IDS/IPS alerts** (signature or anomaly), **full packet capture** (rare, expensive).

steps.title: Patterns
steps.body: **Scan**: one source, many ports/hosts, small packets, short flows. **Beaconing**: regular intervals with small, similar sizes to one destination. **Exfiltration**: large outbound volume, unusual hours, odd destinations. **DNS tunnelling**: very long/high-entropy subdomains, many TXT queries to one domain.

steps.title: Defensive scope
